title: Wisdom's Extension of the Heavens
english: In his understanding, God stretched out the heavens. This was not by chance, for Scripture says in Proverbs that God founded the earth by wisdom and established the heavens by understanding. Therefore there is a divine understanding that belongs to God, and it is to be sought only in Christ Jesus, because all that is of God is Christ: he is God's wisdom, he is God of God, he is God's righteousness, he is sanctification, he is redemption, and thus he is also God's understanding. Though the underlying reality is one, we speak of it with many names according to our thoughts; thus we do not think the same thing about Christ when we call him wisdom as when we call him righteousness. When we think of him as wisdom, we receive the knowledge of divine and human things; when we think of him as righteousness, we receive the power that distributes according to worth in all things; when we think of him as sanctification, we receive the perfecting power that makes the holy ones become believers devoted to God. Likewise, we think of him as understanding when understanding is the knowledge of good, evil, and indifferent things. This understanding separates those who dwell in heaven from those who bear the heavenly man, dividing evil from good so that the heaven may not be polluted — for it is the heaven that has been stretched out by God's understanding, and the righteous person is also called heaven, as it is written: 'And he stretched out the heaven by his understanding.' How then is the heaven stretched out? Wisdom stretches it out, as when it is said, 'Since I stretched out words and you did not pay attention,' indicating an extension of speech; thus the heaven is stretched out by wisdom. It is also said in the Psalms: 'He stretches out the heaven like a skin,' and our soul, previously contracted, is stretched out so that it may receive God's wisdom. But let us return to our point: we were saying that the heaven came into being by understanding, and those who bear the heavenly man are themselves heaven. For to the sinner it is said, 'You are earth, and to earth you shall go,' but this would not be said to the righteous one, of whom it is said, 'The kingdom of heaven is his'; instead, it is said to him, 'You are heaven, and to heaven you shall go.' Or, if one bears the earthly image, it is said, 'You are earth, and to earth you shall go'; but if one bears the heavenly image, it is no longer fitting to say, 'You are earth, and to earth you shall go.' You are heaven, and to heaven you shall go. Therefore each of us has heavenly works and earthly works. Earthly works are those which the hoarder brings down to the kindred earth upon the earth and does not store up in heaven; heavenly works are those by which the one who stores up in heaven, the one who bore 'the image of the heavenly,' lifts up the kindred places in heaven, doing things according to virtue.

The passage emphasizes that divine attributes such as wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption are not separate qualities but are all identical with Christ, who is the one Wisdom and Power of God. Understanding, as one of these attributes, is thus also Christ himself. The stretching of the heavens by understanding is not a physical act but a metaphorical expression of how divine wisdom orders and expands the realm of the spirit, just as words are stretched out when they are spoken but not heeded. The soul must be expanded like a skin to receive this wisdom, and those who live righteously, bearing the heavenly image, are themselves heaven and destined for heaven, while those who cling to earthly things remain bound to the earth. Thus the faithful have both heavenly and earthly responsibilities: they must store up treasures in heaven by virtuous living, not merely accumulate goods on earth.

title: The Saints as Clouds of Divine Truth
english: He led forth clouds from the ends of the earth. This saying was formerly in the Psalm and we have said it, how God 'led forth clouds clouds from the ends of the earth,' which things it is necessary to repeat, for those who know for remembrance and recall of what was said, and for those who have forgotten or not encountered it for clarity of this, whether it is being revealed and made manifest or at any time being understood.

We said moreover that the saints are clouds. For 'your truth of the clouds' cannot be referred to the inanimate clouds, but the truth of God extends to the clouds, which hear the command of God and know where to send forth rain and from whom to withhold it; for as clouds being, to which God commands not to rain or to rain, it is written 'I command the clouds not to rain rain upon him.'

Then concerning these clouds, if no rain, God does not command the clouds not to rain upon the vineyard or the land rain, but altogether no cloud appears, as it is written in the third of the Kings. Where in the time of drought a cloud did not appear, when according to the word of the prophecy of Elijah the rain was about to come to be, there appeared a trace of a cloud 'as the trace of a man' and it became a cloud producing the rain.

As therefore the clouds existing and being commanded not to rain when the soul of the rain is unworthy, it is said 'I command the clouds not to rain rain upon him.' Therefore each of the saints is a cloud. Moses was a cloud and as a cloud he said: 'Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak; and let the earth hear the words of my mouth. Let my utterance be waited for as rain. If I were not a cloud, never would I have spoken. As rain my utterance, and let my words descend as dew.'

As a cloud he says: 'As rain upon the grass, and as snow upon the herb, because I have proclaimed the name of the Lord.' Thus as a cloud and Isaiah says: 'Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken.' And because he himself was a cloud, cloud, he spoke of the clouds those who prophesy with him, saying as he prophesies: 'I command the clouds not to rain rain upon him.'

title: God Draws Clouds from the Last of the Earth
english: If we have considered what the clouds are, let us examine how God draws up clouds from the farthest part of the earth. How from 'the farthest part of the earth'? The Savior says: 'Whoever wishes to be first among you shall be last of all.' Paul observed this commandment and was last in this world; therefore he says: 'I think that God has displayed the apostles as last, as men doomed to death, for we have become a spectacle to the world and to angels and to men.' Therefore, whoever keeps the Savior's commandment and becomes last as regards the life of this one becomes a cloud; and God draws up clouds not from the first of the earth, nor from consular ones, nor from leaders, nor from the rich, for 'Blessed are the poor, for theirs is the kingdom of God.' You see how God draws up from the last and forms the clouds into bodies; therefore, if we wish to become clouds upon which the truth of God reaches, we must become last of all and declare in work and disposition: 'I think that God has displayed us the apostles as last' (even if I am not an apostle, it is permitted for me to become last, so that God, drawing up clouds from 'the farthest part of the earth,' may draw me up). And He made lightning for rain. Those who are clever about these things say that the generation of lightning occurs from clouds rubbing against one another.

For just as it happens with fiery stones thrown upon the earth, when one or two stones strike each other and fire is kindled, so they say it happens with the clouds: when the clouds strike together during winter, lightning occurs. Hence, as lightning always occurs together with thunder, the thunder manifests the sound of the clouds' collision, and the lightning produces the light.
translator_notes: In [p3], the phrase 'ἵνα ὁ θεὸς ἀνάγων νεφέλας 241r | ἀπ' «ἐσχάτου τῆς γῆς«' appears to contain a folio reference ('241r') and a possible OCR artifact ('|'); the Greek is treated as readable despite the intrusion. The lemma list includes load-bearing theological and physical terms; abstract concepts like 'δικαιοσύνη' are included due to their thematic role in the Beatitude context, though not explicitly stated in the Greek.

title: The Cloud and Lightning of Scripture
english: If you have understood the example, look also at the intelligible cloud. Moses was a cloud, Joshua the son of Nun was a cloud. These two speak to one another, and from their words lightning comes. Jeremiah was a cloud, Baruch was a cloud. They converse with each other, and lightning came from the words of Jeremiah and the words of Baruch. So if you are able, gather from the writings how lightning comes. And in the new covenant Paul and Silvanus were two clouds.

They came together, and the lightning of the letter occurred. 'Lightnings' therefore God 'made into rain and brought forth winds from his treasuries.' Are then these winds in the treasuries? Or does it not appear how their nature, blowing upon the earth, subsists? But there are treasuries of winds, treasuries of spirits: 'spirit of wisdom and understanding, spirit of counsel and might, spirit of knowledge and godliness,' 'spirit of the fear of the Lord,' 'spirit of power and love and sound mind.' And you yourself are able from the writings to gather these winds. These spirits are in the treasuries. What are the treasuries? 'in whom are hid the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.' These treasuries are in Christ.

Therefore from thence come these winds, these spirits, that the one may be wise, the other faithful, the other having knowledge, the other having received some gift of God. 'For to one is given by the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit, and to another faith in the same Spirit'.

title: The Resurrection and the Divine Treasuries
english: He brought up clouds from the ends of the earth, made lightnings for rain, and brought forth winds from his storehouses. We, through God, hope to reach these storehouses. Since there are many such storehouses, there will be rest in them for those who are stirred up. What I say is such.

The resurrection of the dead occurs in certain orders, for the apostle says: 'each in his own order.' Since the orders are not mixed together by chance, one order will be in one of God's storehouses, another in another, and a third in yet another. Yet all these storehouses have one storehouse in which they dwell.

Therefore it is said by Paul: 'in whom are the storehouses of wisdom and knowledge hidden.' Just as I seek the one precious pearl through many pearls, so I come to the treasury of treasuries, the Lord of lords, the King of kings, when I shall be worthy of the spirits from God's treasuries, for he brought forth winds from his storehouses.
translator_notes: In p1, the word 'καταντή- σεσθαι' appears to be a line-broken OCR artifact for 'καταντήσεσθαι'; restored accordingly. The phrase 'ἕνα πολύτι- μον μαργαρίτην' is line-broken; restored as 'ἕνα πολύτιμον μαργαρίτην'. No invented Greek is used.

title: Human wisdom is folly before divine knowledge
english: All humanity has been made foolish by knowledge, for if everyone is made foolish by knowledge and Paul is a human, then Paul too was made foolish by partial knowledge—seeing only in part, as through a mirror dimly—and if it could be said, he perceived and comprehended the things of existence in manifold and even infinite ways.

Yet from the opposing view, when we consider the sins of Jerusalem and the sins of Sodom, and compare the lesser transgressions, the righteousness of Sodom appears in relation to Jerusalem's iniquities, as Paul declares: 'Sodom has been justified by you.'

Thus, just as the sins of Sodom are not righteousness, but righteousness emerges only in contrast to greater injustice, so too Paul’s knowledge, when measured against the divine knowledge that dwells in the heavens, is revealed as folly before perfect knowledge.

Therefore, the saying holds: 'All humanity has been made foolish by knowledge.' I believe the Preacher perceived this truth when he lamented: 'I said, I will become wise,' but wisdom withdrew far from him, vanishing into a deep abyss—who can find it?

title: The Foolishness of God as True Wisdom
english: The discourse is about to dare to say that the one who came in the flesh emptied himself so that the cosmos might be filled by his emptiness. If he emptied himself by that which came in the flesh, then that emptiness was wisdom.

For the foolishness of God is wiser than men. If I had said 'the foolishness of God,' how could the contentious have accused me? How could they have blamed me? How, if the things said were considered good and even beautiful by them, but this, as they think, was not well said, could I have been accused for saying 'the foolishness of God'?

But now Paul, as wise and possessing apostolic authority, dared to say that all earthly wisdom, and that in himself and in Peter and the apostles, all wisdom that has come into the world, is 'the foolishness of God.'
For as regards that wisdom which no earthly place can contain, as regards that heavenly, supra-cosmic wisdom, this incarnate foolishness of God is such.

But this 'the foolishness of God is wiser than men.' Of which men? Not the foolish, but it is wiser even than the wise. Even if you speak of the wise of this age, whether rulers or prophets, the rulers of this age 'the foolishness of God,' as I have said, 'is wiser than men.'

title: The Weakness of God Overcomes Worldly Wisdom
english: The discourse introduces a paradox: that the wisdom of the world is foolishness before God, and that God has made foolish the wisdom of the world.
It questions whether divine wisdom must contend with worldly wisdom or if only a little of God’s foolishness is needed to expose and overcome it.
It illustrates that even a small measure of God’s so-called foolishness surpasses all human wisdom, just as divine weakness exceeds human strength.
Through Christ, believers are empowered from weakness and made wise by divine foolishness so that they may ascend to God’s wisdom and strength, to whom be glory and might forever. Amen.

title: The Universal Presence of the Word
english: The historical presence of our Lord Jesus Christ has resulted in a universal bodily sojourn that has shone throughout the world, when 'the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.' For the true light that enlightens every person coming into the world was present.

In the world that was made through Him, and the world did not know Him. He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him. But it is necessary to know that He also previously dwelled, even if not bodily, in each of the saints, and after this visible sojourn He again dwells among us. And if you wish to obtain proof, pay attention to the Word spoken to Jeremiah by the Lord saying, 'Hear and the following.' For what is 'the Word spoken by the Lord' whether to Jeremiah or Isaiah or Ezekiel or to anyone else, or the one in the beginning to God? I do not know another Word of the Lord besides this, about which the evangelist said 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.'

title: Covenant and Spiritual Liberation
english: The word is addressed to men of Judah, to those dwelling in Jerusalem. This is the church.

For the city of God is the church, the vision of peace, in which peace is present, which we have brought, if we are children of peace, it increases and is seen. Therefore, hear the words of this covenant, and speak to men of Judah and those dwelling in Jerusalem. And you will say to them: Thus says the Lord God of Israel, a man who does not hear the words of the covenant which I commanded your fathers; who especially hears 'the words of the covenant which the God commanded your fathers'? Does the believer in him or those who do not believe in Moses, shown by not believing in the Lord? For the Savior says to them: 'If you believe in Moses, you would believe in me, for he wrote about me. If you do not believe in his writings, how will you believe in my words?' Therefore, those did not believe in Moses, but we believe in Christ, and we believe in the covenant through Moses, and it is said to us that we may not be cursed; cursed is the man who does not hear the words of the covenant which I commanded your fathers.

title: God's People and the Living Covenant
english: We have become God's people, and the righteousness of God is to the people from the nations. For this is the people that is born in entirety, and it is said in the prophet: 'If a nation was born once, a nation was born once when the savior appeared and thousands believed in one day, and were added on another day three thousand. And it is seen that the whole people is born by the word of God and the barren woman, who previously did not bear, is being born in entirety, to whom it is said: 'Rejoice, barren one who does not bear, break forth and cry, you who do not wail, for many are the children of the desolate rather than of the one who has a husband.' The desolate is the church; the desolate is God's law. The one who has a husband is that synagogue which is called the congregation.

What then does God promise me? 'You shall be to me a people, and I shall be to you a God.' Not all are God, but only those to whom He grants Himself, as He granted Himself to that patriarch to whom He said, 'I am your God,' and again to another, 'I shall be your God,' and concerning others, 'I shall be their God.' When then do we attain, as I say individually, to being His God? If you wish to know what God is and to whom He grants His name, He is the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob. And the Savior says this: 'God is not of the dead but of the living.' Who is the dead? The sinner, the one not having the one who spoke.

I am the one having dead works, the one not yet having repented from dead works, about which the apostle says: 'Do not lay again a foundation of repentance from dead works.' If then 'God is not a God of the dead but of the living,' and we know who is the living, because the one living according to Christ and remaining with Him, if we desire one of us to be God, we will put away the works of death, that He may fulfill His promise saying: 'And I shall be to you a God, that I may establish my oath which I swore to your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey.' For He says: 'I shall establish my oath which I swore to your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey,' as not yet having given them the 'land flowing with milk and honey.' For this is not the land which God said 'flowing with milk and honey,' but that which the Savior taught saying: 'Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the land.'

title: Curses and Bonds of Sin
english: Then the prophet responds to the Lord's words, saying, 'Cursed is the man who does not listen to the words of this covenant.' And I answered, 'Let it be, Lord. What does 'Let it be, Lord' mean? Cursed is the one who does not remain in the words of this covenant.'

The Lord said to me, 'Know these words in the cities of Judah and outside Jerusalem. We read the words of God in the cities of Judah and outside Jerusalem, inviting them to salvation. 'Hear these words and do them,' but they did not. The Lord said to me, 'A bond of sin has been found among men of Judah and those living in Jerusalem.'

Some phrases in p5 and p7 require contextual interpretation due to fragmented syntax.

title: Divine Teaching and the Teacher
english: If divine words are present in the Law and Prophets, and also in the Gospels and Apostles, the one being taught must have God as the teacher of divine words, for God is the one who teaches knowledge, as written in Psalms. The Savior also testifies that no one should be called a teacher on earth, saying, 'And you should not call anyone on earth your teacher, for one is your teacher, the Father in heaven.' The Father who teaches either through Himself or through Christ or in the Holy Spirit or through Paul or through Peter or through some other holy one, may it be said, only the Spirit of God and the Word of God should dwell and teach. What is this said for? Because the prophet says, 'Reveal Yourself to me, Lord, that I may know,' for I will not know unless You reveal Yourself to me, and when You reveal Yourself to me, I will see their deeds and understand what each person does and of what kind their choices are.

This is what the prophet says. Then let us see what the Savior says in the prophet: 'I was like a harmless lamb led to be sacrificed and I did not know. They plotted against me, saying, 'Come, let us put a stick into his bread, and cut him off from the land of the living, and his name will no longer be remembered.' As the prophet Isaiah says, 'The Christ was led to slaughter like a lamb, and as a sheep before the shearer is silent, so He did not open His mouth.'

There Isaiah speaks about Him, but here Christ speaks about Himself, saying, 'I was like a harmless lamb led to be sacrificed and I did not know.' He did not say what he did not know. For he did not say, 'I did not know evils,' nor 'I did not know goods,' nor 'I did not know sin,' but simply 'I did not know.' Therefore, you must investigate what He did not know. Learn what He did not know from 'The one who did not know sin, He made sin for us.' For to know sin is to commit sin, just as to know righteousness is to act righteously. Therefore, the one who announces things about righteousness and does not act righteously does not know righteousness.

title: The Wood in the Bread
english: They conceived a plan, saying, 'Come, let us cast wood into his bread.' For indeed the Jews crucified him, which we boldly proclaim. How does this apply to 'They conceived a plan against me, saying, 'Come, let us cast wood into his bread'? It is an act to understand. The bread of Jesus is the word in which we are nourished.

Therefore, when he taught in the people, they wished to add a stumbling block to his teaching through his crucifixion, saying, 'Let us cast wood into his bread.' For when the crucifixion is added to the word of Jesus' teaching, wood is cast into his bread.

I will say something more paradoxical: the wood cast into his bread made the bread better. I take an example from Moses' law: the wood cast into bitter water made it sweet. Thus the wood of Jesus Christ's passion made his bread sweeter. Before the wood came into his bread, when the bread alone existed and no wood was in his teaching, 'his voice did not go out to all the earth.' But when the bread received power through the wood cast into it, therefore his teaching's word spread throughout the whole world.
I said, 'Come, let us cast wood into his bread.'
translator_notes: Possible OCR error: 'προσ-έλαβεν' likely 'προσέλαβεν' (received).
Uncertain line breaks in p3: 'ἐγὼ γὰρ λέγω ὅτι' may belong to previous paragraph.

title: The Grain of Wheat and the Fruit of Death
english: They say, 'Let us cut him off from the land of the living, and his name will no longer be remembered.' Thus they killed him, as if erasing his name. But Jesus knows how he dies and why. Therefore he says, 'If the grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; if it dies, it bears much fruit.' So the death of Jesus becomes a stalk of wheat, producing abundant and plentiful sown seed.

As if hypothetically he were not crucified or died, the grain of wheat would have remained alone, and many would not have come from it. Consider his word, if he does not intend this: 'The grain of wheat, if it does not fall into the earth and die, remains alone; if it dies, it bears much fruit.' The death of Jesus bore fruit for all, and if the death bore so much, how many will the resurrection bear?

title: Judgment on Anathoth and the Loss of Divine Word
english: Lord of powers judging justly, testing kidneys and hearts, I seek vengeance from them. This is a prophetic prayer, to see vengeance from them, for Jerusalem is surrounded by armies, its desolation declared, and it is said to them: 'Behold, your house is forsaken.' I will see vengeance in them, for I have revealed my cause to you.

Behold, I will visit them; their youths will die by the sword, and their sons and daughters will die by famine. No remnant will remain of them, upon those dwelling in Anathoth in the year of their visitation. For the name of Anathoth is taken here. The whole Jewish mystery is spoken tropically in it, for Anathoth means 'Listening.'

Since listening to God was in that people, as also the kingdom of God, and the kingdom was said to be taken from them and given to a people producing its fruits, thus it happened also to 'the men of Anathoth,' those in the Listening, seeking the soul. Not Jeremiah (for the history does not say that men of Anathoth sought Jeremiah's soul. We have the Books, the Scripture remembers Jeremiah there, nothing such is said in them nor in the Apocrypha. We have the prophet's book, the men of Anathoth have not said anything), but these are said about Christ. 'Those seeking my soul, saying, 'You will not prophesy in the name of the Lord.'
The Jews hindered teaching about Jesus. 'If not, he will die in our hands.'

Behold, I will visit them; their youths will die by the sword, and their sons and daughters will die by famine. They did not die by the sword then, but after the present presence, famine came upon them, not a famine of bread or thirst for water, but a famine of the word of the Lord, for 'Thus says the Lord Almighty' is no longer said among them. This famine, that prophecy no longer is, and what do I say, prophecy? Neither teaching. Even if wise men frequent them, there is no longer the word of the Lord among them, for it is fulfilled that 'The Lord has taken from Judah and from Jerusalem the strong and the mighty, the giant and the strong, and the warrior and the judge and the prophet and the thinker and the elder and the commander and the wonderful counselor and the wise architect and the discerning listener.'
translator_notes: Bracketed sections may indicate citations or editorial insertions. Some passages show possible OCR errors (e.g., 'ἐπισκέψομαι ἐπ αὐτούς' with missing space).

title: The Prosperity of the Wicked and Divine Justice
english: The people there are abandoned, for evil has come upon those dwelling in Anathoth during their year of visitation. Righteous are you, Lord, that I may defend myself before you; I will declare my judgments before you. Why does the way of the wicked prosper? The transgressors have become upright.

We still inquire whether God, who gave the law and the prophets, is good, seeing that the way of the wicked prospers and the wicked are not punished. All who transgressed have become upright. Those who speak against the creator, slandering him, have prospered, been planted, and taken root, and have borne fruit. What fruit did Magion's offspring produce, or Basilides', or Valentinus'? This is what is prophesied and spoken about the wicked: 'They have begotten and produced fruit.' 'You are near to their mouth, but far from their kidneys,' they name the name of Jesus, yet do not have Jesus, for they do not confess him as they should. And you, Lord, know me, have seen me, tested my heart before you; purify them for the day of their slaughter. What shall I do, that I may make this clear? The purification of the punished is called the punishment of the condemned; 'purify them for the day,' he says, 'of their slaughter. Through their slaughter, purify them; for whom the Lord loves, he disciplines, and all sons he accepts are scourged.'
translator_notes: Uncertain reading 'ἐπάξζ' possibly 'ἐπάξιν' (reproach).
Possible OCR error in 'ἐποίησαν' (omitted in original text).
Bracketed text '〈καὶ ἐποίησαν〉' indicates uncertainty in the original.

title: Earth's Grief and Joy
english: The earth and the vegetation of the field will wither from the wickedness of those dwelling within it, as if the earth itself mourns due to the wrongdoing of those who traverse it.

Similarly, water and the angel assigned over it are discussed, for the earth mourns or does not mourn; the earth itself is not grieving from its inhabitants, but consider the ordered arrangement of all things set upon the earth, and another set over waters, another over air, and a fourth over fire.

title: Abandonment and Passion of Christ
english: I have abandoned my house, I have left my inheritance, I have given my beloved soul into the hands of its enemies. Behold the one existing in the form of God, who is in the heavens, behold his heavenly house. If you wish to see higher (for he is in the Father's), behold his house being God.

For that was his inheritance, the lands with the angels, the order with the holy powers. I have given my beloved soul into the hands of its enemies. He delivered his soul into the hands of the enemies of the soul, into the hands of Jews who killed him, into the hands of rulers who conspired against him, into the hands of kings, when 'the kings of the earth stood and the rulers conspired together against the Lord and against his Christ.'

title: Inheritance as a Lion in the Forest
english: My inheritance became to me like a lion in the forest. The earthly inheritance of the one who was plundered by it, and the inheritance of the Jews, having been wilded, seeks to devour Jesus and slander him and conspire against those who believe in him.

He gave upon me her voice, therefore I hated her. Does my inheritance become a hyena's den? The inheritance has become a hyena's den, the most savage, the corpse-eating, the one that dwells by monuments, the one that eats mortal bodies. Does my inheritance become a hyena's den?

The beasts of the field have come, they devour that people. See their hearts being devoured by opposing powers. If Jesus did not fear them but said, 'Go, gather the beasts,' how much more will he not fear us? If we do not perform the law of God, the word of the gospel, he will again say, 'Go, gather the beasts and deliver them.'

We will confess our transgressions repenting, and we will not be delivered to beasts, but to holy angels who carry us, transferring us from this age to the coming one in Christ Jesus, to whom is the power and glory forever. Amen.

title: Through Christ the whole land was made desolate
english: Who is the one saying, 'Through me the whole land was made desolate with desolation'? Christ says these things. Before his sojourn many sins had indeed come to the people, but not of such a kind that they should be abandoned altogether and handed over to a long captivity. But when they filled up 'the measure of their fathers' and added to killing the prophets and pursuing the righteous the killing of 'the Christ of God,' then what was spoken came to be: 'Your house is left to you.' And because of him they have suffered these things, and 'with desolation the whole land was made desolate.'
translator_notes: OCR gap ἀποκτεῖ-Mitte ναι read as ἀποκτεῖναι.

title: The earth in you made desolate when Jesus comes
english: But if you also want to hear something higher than 'Through me the whole land was made desolate with desolation,' look at the earth in you—how it was made desolate when Jesus came. For it was made desolate when 'the members that are upon the earth' were put to death, and the earth no longer works its own works. No longer do the works of the flesh spring up in the righteous, with which the flesh used to flourish—no longer fornication, no longer uncleanness, no longer sensuality, no idolatry, no sorcery, and the rest. And the Savior also says: 'Do you think that I came to cast peace upon the earth? I did not come to cast peace but a sword.' Truly, before he came there was no sword upon the earth, nor did 'the flesh desire against the Spirit, nor the Spirit against the flesh.' But when he came and we were taught what belongs to the flesh and what to the Spirit, the teaching, become like a sword on earth, divided the flesh and the earth from the Spirit. And 'the earth was made desolate' when we carry about the putting-to-death of Jesus in the body, and we no longer live according to flesh, but the Spirit lives, and we sow nothing into the flesh but everything into the Spirit, so that we may not reap corruption from the flesh but from the Spirit eternal life.
translator_notes: Lacuna τῶν ἐπὶ τῆς < supplied as τῆς γῆς from Pauline parallel (Col 3:5).

title: Sowing wheat and reaping thorns; lots that do not save
english: It is said to those who have sinned: 'Sow wheat and reap thorns.' For even if they deal with the oracles of God, those who do not deal with them well, nor live as they ought, nor believe, sow wheat and reap thorns. Especially this can be understood of the heterodox who meet the Scriptures and reap thorns not from the Scriptures but from their own inventions. 'Their lots will not benefit them.' Others have also explained these things. And since we do not reject their explanation, we fairly bring it into the open—not as ourselves discovering it but as having learned a good lesson. This word will benefit both you and us if we pay attention to what is written—we who seem to be of a certain lot, seated in front of you, so that some want to come into this lot.
But know that the lot does not save in every case. For many elders too will perish, and many of the laity will be shown blessed.

Since then there are some in the lot who do not live so as to be benefited and to adorn the lot, therefore, say those who explained it, it is written: 'Their lots will not benefit them.' For what benefits is not the mere sitting in the eldership, but living worthily of the place, as the word requires. The word requires you also to live well, and us. But if one may put it so—'the mighty will be examined mightily'—more is required of me than of the deacon, more of the deacon than of the layperson, and the one entrusted with the rule of us all, the church's rule itself, is required still more. Therefore the apostle who was entrusted with great things says—listen—'Let a person regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God.'
Here then seek among the stewards that someone faithful be found. And so rare it is to find a steward faithful and good.

Jesus, 'who knows all things before their coming to be,' says: 'Who then is the faithful and prudent steward, whom his lord will set over his household to give the measure of grain to his servants in season?' Then he blames certain stewards and says: 'But if that wicked servant begins to say, “My lord delays to come,” and begins to beat his fellow servants and the maidservants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, the lord of that servant will come on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in two, and assign his portion with the unfaithful.' So much for 'Their lots will not benefit them.'

title: Be ashamed of empty boasting before the Lord
english: Let us also look at the necessary rebuke next, which it is good to take up in the ethical place, saying: 'Be ashamed of your boasting, of reproach before the Lord.' There are things in which we boast through folly, though they are not worthy of boasting. For example, if someone boasts that he is rich and possesses much, one might say to him: 'Be ashamed of your boasting.'

If someone boasts of this outward nobility, it will be said to him: 'Be ashamed of your boasting.' If someone boasts of costly clothing, of a house built richly, that boasting is foreign to the boasting of the saints; therefore it will be said to such a one: 'Be ashamed of your boasting.' Hear the word of the prophet Jeremiah commanding us not to boast even in wisdom: 'Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom,' he says, 'nor the strong in his strength, nor the rich in his wealth, but let the one who boasts boast in this: understanding and knowing that I am the Lord.' Do you want to boast and, boasting, not hear 'Be ashamed of your boasting'? Boast as the apostle and say: 'Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me and I to the world.' Do you want to boast so that it may not be said, 'Be ashamed of your boasting'? Hear Paul boasting and learn when he says: 'Most gladly then will I boast in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may tabernacle upon me.' Hear what kinds of boasts he boasts: 'In labors more abundantly'—which of us can say this?—'in prisons beyond measure, in deaths often.'

'Five times I received from the Jews forty lashes less one; three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; three times I was shipwrecked.' So we learn that there are also differences among boastings—some boastings worthy of shame, of which that apostolic word might be said: 'And their glory is in their shame'—things of which they ought to be ashamed, and about these they suppose they are glorified.

title: The linen belt: Israel cast off, the church girded on
english: After these things let us look at what concerns the belt. For 'thus says the Lord: Go and get yourself a linen belt, and put it around your waist, and you shall not pass it through water.' And I got a belt according to the word of the Lord and put it around my waist. And the word of the Lord came to me saying: 'Take the belt that is around your waist, and rise and go to the Euphrates, and hide it there in the cleft of the rock.' After days he goes there and finds this belt rotten. And the Lord adds, giving the occasion for interpreting the belt, saying: 'As the belt is glued to a man's waist, so I glued to myself the house of Israel and the whole house of Judah, says the Lord, to become for me a people named and a boast and a glory—and they did not listen to me.' So the prophet is taken in God's place, girding the linen belt around his waist, as God girded the people: 'For I glued this people to myself,' he says—as if the people becomes God's belt.

But why does it become God's belt around his waist? Let the one able, reading Ezekiel and seeing God as it were embodied by the word—and how what is from the waist downward is fire, and what is from the waist is electrum—search out the word, why what is below God is fire. The matters from the waist and from generation—these are fire. For everything in generation needs the cleansing that comes from fire; everything in generation needs chastisement. But what is above the waist and has gone beyond generation—these are matter as in what is purest and most precious; for electrum is said to be more valuable than gold.

Since then Scripture uses examples in order to teach that God's body above is more honorable and the body below is lesser, for this reason it introduced God composed of fire and electrum. And each of us in generation is fire; we are not the electrum. But if we ascend and make progress—for it is possible to move from being today among the things below, so as to become God's body above—we will be, having crossed the fire, the electrum around God's higher body. So he glues around his waist the linen belt.

To what end? That it may be shown that the people is as it were a covering of God. For against those who want to accuse God the people stands and as it were shields him and does not allow anything out of place to be said about God. But when we sin, just as the prophet puts this belt away and condemns it to the Euphrates river so that it may be destroyed there, so the one who sins is cast away from God's waist, and having been cast out is thrown into the Euphrates river—the river of Mesopotamia, where the Assyrians are enemies to Israel, where the Babylonians are—and there he is destroyed. For though there are so many rivers, the prophet is sent from Judea to the Euphrates river to deal with and lead away a linen belt.

And why also 'linen'? Because it has its origin from earth; for it is a plant rising from earth, then after being cultivated it is carded and washed and scrubbed and made with much working, so that it may become such as to be a belt or whatever else. We too then all have our origin as God's belt, and having our origin from earth we need much preparation, that we may be carded, that we may be washed, that we may put away the color of the earth. For the color of linen's origin is one thing, and that from the working another. The color of linen's origin is rather black, but from the working it becomes most bright. Something of this kind also reaches us who are in generation. We are black according to the beginning in believing; therefore at the beginning of the Song of Songs it is said: 'I am black and beautiful.' And we at the start resemble Ethiopians in the soul. Then we are scrubbed clean, that we may become brighter according to 'Who is this who comes up whitened?' And we become 'bright and clean linen,' then also we are woven onto God's belt when we are worthy to be glued to God. God does not put us away. He put away the first people—'the whole house of Judah' and 'the house of Israel.'

It came to be so as not to be used any longer; for he no longer girds them around himself. In their place God has girded us; for having cast off the belt he did not remain naked, but wove another belt for himself. This belt is the church from the nations—which should know that 'if God did not spare the former, how much more will he not spare her either if she sins,' unless she is worthy of God's waist. 'But the one glued to the Lord is one spirit' in Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the power forever. Amen.
translator_notes: Corrupt daggered phrase on God's body left unrestored; sense from surrounding Ezekiel image.

title: Every wineskin will be filled with wine
english: What the prophet is commanded by God to say ought to be worthy of God. Yet if we remain on the letter it does not appear worthy of God, so that someone hearing the letter might say: these letters are folly. But a psychic person will say this; for 'the psychic person does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are folly to him.'

Look then at what the wording says. 'And you shall say to this people: Thus says the Lord the God of Israel'—what 'the Lord the God of Israel' says, let it be worthy of the Lord of Israel—'Every wineskin will be filled with wine. And if they say to you, “Shall we not know, knowing, that every wineskin will be filled with wine?”' And those who answer, if they say these things standing on the bare wording, claim to know that 'every wineskin will be filled with wine,' and they lie. For not every wineskin will be filled with wine. There are wineskins filled with oil or with some other liquid substance. So some lie; for not every wineskin will be filled with wine. And the people answers saying: 'Shall we not know, knowing, that every wineskin will be filled with wine?'—words that will receive an interpretation of this kind, as far as we can.

If we know the differences among wines and what is said about them, and accordingly look at the wineskins, we will see that it is true that every wineskin will be filled with wine. For whether someone is good—let us name him so among wineskins, a wineskin—he will be filled with wine according to his own goodness. Or whether he is, by comparison of wineskins and the judgment about them, wicked, he too according to his wickedness will be filled with wicked wine. How then can we take from Scripture the different wines? About the worse ones it is written like this: 'For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their shoot from Gomorrah.

Their grape is a grape of gall; a cluster of bitterness to them; their wine is the rage of dragons, and the incurable rage of asps.' And about the better ones: 'Your cup that makes drunk is as the strongest,' and Wisdom calls to her own mixing-bowl saying: 'Come, eat my bread, and drink the wine I have mixed for you.' So there is wine from Sodom, and there is wine that Wisdom mixes. And again: 'A vineyard came to be for the beloved on a horn in a rich place,' planted by God, the vine called Sorek—choice and marvelous. And there is also a vine of the Egyptians, which God strikes according to what is written: that 'God struck their vine with hail, and their mulberry trees with frost.'

title: Day for work; night when no one can work
english: Perhaps we will understand what is written by using a Gospel saying spoken by the Savior that runs like this: 'Work while it is day; night comes when no one can work.' There he named day this age (but I necessarily added 'there'; for I know that other things are indicated to others elsewhere); so he named day this age, and darkness and night the consummation because of the punishments. For 'Why do you desire the day of the Lord? And this is darkness and not light,' says Amos the prophet.

If you see what is grim after the consummation of the world—what follows as almost the whole race of human beings are punished for what was sinned—you will see that what surrounds then grew dark, and no longer can anyone glorify God, if indeed the word of God also commanded the righteous saying: 'Go, my people, enter into your storeroom, shut your door, hide yourself a little while, until my wrath of anger passes.' And together with these things, if anyone can, let him observe that he said 'a little while.' But that 'little' is little to God; it is not little to a human being. For one must see that for each there is something little and great. And from an example I will show that for each there is something little or great.

For each living thing food of such-and-such amount is little by comparison with its constitution, and much food of such-and-such amount again by comparison with its makeup. And so what is little for a human being is great for another living thing. What is little, say, for a man is much for a child. So the whole time of human life is a little time, and that of one long-lived, as toward the whole of the present age. So also what is little to God is much toward us, and a whole age is God's little.

If then it is said: 'Go, my people, enter into your storerooms, shut your door, hide yourself a little while,' that little must be thought said not toward the relation of the one commanded to go and enter his own storerooms, but toward the relation of the one commanding these things, to whom what is much to this one is little. For if until the wrath of God's anger passes some must enter their own storerooms, and there are those for whom sins are not forgiven not only through this whole age but also through the whole age to come, clearly that little stretches alongside what was said.

title: Glory to God by deeds, not by little words
english: 'Give' then 'glory to the Lord our God.' How do we give glory to the Lord our God? I do not seek giving glory to the Lord our God in voices and little words, but in deeds the one who gives glory to the Lord God gives glory to him. In temperance glorify God; in righteousness, in well-doing glorify God; give glory to God in courage and endurance; give glory to God in piety and holiness and the remaining virtues. And if these things are so and someone thus glorifies God, if I say the opposites, do not think I blaspheme; for I will also set Scripture as witness of those.

The temperate glorifies God; the intemperate dishonors God. For like Nebuchadnezzar he overturns the temple of God and 'destroys the temple of God' and 'through the transgression of the law dishonors God' (this wording too is apostolic). So the sinner puts dishonor around God. And questions about providence are sought, so that some doubt whether there is providence—for no other reason than through wickedness. Take away wickedness, and you do not stumble at providence. But those who stumble at providence say these things up and down: why so many adulterers and so many soft ones, why so many atheists and impious? And those who generated the dishonor for providence, the stumbling-blocks for God, the blasphemy against the one who made the world, are the sinners. So some give glory to God; but those who do the things contrary to God's glory through sins give no glory to God.

title: Bright mountains and dark; hear the law in a hidden way
english: 'Give glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, before your feet stumble on dark mountains.' There are dark mountains; there are bright mountains. Bright mountains are the holy angels of God, the prophets, Moses the servant, the apostles of Jesus Christ. All these are bright mountains, and about these I think it has been said in the Psalms: 'His foundations are in the holy mountains.' And what are dark mountains? Those who lift up heights against the knowledge of God.

The devil is a dark mountain; the rulers of this age who are being abolished are dark mountains; and the demon of epilepsy was a mountain, and it was a dark mountain, about which the Savior said: 'You will say to this mountain.' For when the account of epilepsy was being sought and the disciples said, 'Why could we not cast it out?' the Savior answers that 'If you have faith as a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain'—about which you put forward the question, about which you sought—'You will say to this: Move from here to there, and it will move.' 'From here' from the human being, 'there' to its own place. So those who stumble do not stumble on bright mountains but on dark mountains, when they come to be with the devil and his angels, the dark mountains. 'And you will wait for light.' Yet it can also be joined to 'Give glory to the Lord our God'—the 'and you will wait for light.'

If you give glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, before your feet stumble on dark mountains, clearly even if it grows dark you will wait for the light and the light will succeed you. But another might say (I do not know whether understanding soundly or not) that even those who stumble 'on dark mountains' will wait among the dark mountains waiting for the light of mercy; for this will seem to be the 'and you will wait for light.' And when someone comes upon the dark mountains, let us see what is there: 'shadow of death.'

Where the dark mountains are, there is a shadow of death generated from the dark mountains themselves. 'And they will be placed into darkness.' 'But if you do not hear in a hidden way, your soul will weep from before insult.' Of those who hear, some hear in a hidden way, and some, even if they hear, do not hear in a hidden way. What then is hearing in a hidden way but 'But we speak God's wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom which God predetermined before the ages for our glory'? And again elsewhere it is said that 'most of God's works are in hidden things.' If I hear the law, I either hear in a hidden way or I do not hear in a hidden way.

The Jew does not hear the law in a hidden way; therefore he is circumcised openly, not knowing that it is not 'the one who is a Jew openly, nor the circumcision openly in flesh.' But the one who hears circumcision in a hidden way will be circumcised in secret; the one who hears the things legislated about the Passover in a hidden way eats from the sheep of Christ—for 'our Passover was sacrificed, Christ'—and knowing what the flesh of the Word is like, and knowing that 'it is true food,' he partakes of it; for he heard the Passover in a hidden way. But this common Jew for this reason killed the Lord Jesus and is still today liable for Jesus' murder, since he heard neither the law nor the prophets in a hidden way.

If you read about the unleavened breads, one can hear the command in a hidden way, and one can hear it openly. As many of you as (for the Passover is near) keep unleavened breads, the bodily unleavened breads, you do not hear the command that says: 'If you do not hear in a hidden way, your soul will weep.' And about the Sabbath women who have not heard the prophet do not hear in a hidden way but hear openly. They do not bathe on the Sabbath day; they return 'to the poor and weak elements,' as if Christ had not sojourned—the one who perfects us and carries us across from the legal elements to the Gospel perfection.

For this reason let us attend, reading the law and the prophets, lest we fall under the prophecy that says: 'But if you do not hear in a hidden way, your soul will weep from before insult.' As many as keep the Jewish fast as not understanding the day of atonement after Jesus Christ's sojourn—you did not hear the atonement in a hidden way, but only openly; for to hear the atonement in a hidden way is to hear how God set Jesus as atonement for our sins, and that 'he is atonement for our sins, not for ours only but also for the whole world.' And even if Gospel parables are read and the hearer is one of those outside, he will not hear them in a hidden way.

But if the hearer is an apostle or one of those entering 'into Jesus' house,' he comes to Jesus, inquires also about the unclearness of the parable, and Jesus interprets it, and that hearer of the Gospel becomes one hearing it in a hidden way, so that his soul may not weep; for the soul of those not hearing in a hidden way weeps.

How marvelously he did not say: you will weep, if you do not hear in a hidden way, but: 'your soul will weep.' There is a weeping of the soul alone weeping, and perhaps the Savior teaches us that weeping when he says: 'There will be the weeping.' And even if he says: 'Woe to those who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep,' he speaks about that weeping which the prophet also threatens here saying: 'But if you do not hear in a hidden way, your soul will weep from before insult.' For when you are insulted, then you will weep and your eyes will bring down tears, because the Lord's flock was crushed. If someone now sees the Jewish things and compares them with the ancient, he will see in what way the Lord's flock was crushed.

For this was once the Lord's flock, and since they judged themselves unworthy, the word turned to the nations. If then that flock of the Lord was crushed, we the wild olive, grafted contrary to its nature into the cultivated olive of the fathers—ought we not fear more, lest this 'flock of the Lord' also be crushed? For it is going to be crushed sometime according to what was said by the Savior, when 'because lawlessness is multiplied the love of many will grow cold.' About whom is the word? Is 'the love of many will grow cold' not said about those called Christians? About whom is the word, that 'When the Son of Man comes, will he find the faith on the earth?' Is it not about us? For this reason let us attend to ourselves, doing everything, that day by day this flock of God may be improved, healed, cured, and every crushing depart from our souls, that we may be perfected in Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the power forever.
Amen.

title: Wineskins of virtue and of punishment
english: Consider with me then that all human beings are now, in a figurative way, able to hold wine. And I name them wineskins in this respect and say that the worthless one is filled with 'wine of the vine of Sodom,' is filled with Egyptian wine and with wine of Israel's enemies, but the holy and benefited one is filled with wine from the vine of Sorek and with wine about which it is written: 'Your cup making drunk as the strongest,' and again the holy one is filled with wine from which Wisdom has mixed. Let these things be understood by me according to vice and virtue, so that 'every wineskin is filled with wine' may be seen. But if we must also see the things that come through vice and through virtue—punishments through vice, blessings and promises through virtue—let us set out from the sacred writings how punishments and promises are called wine: 'Take the cup of this unmixed wine, and you shall make all the nations drink to whom I send you to them.'

Jeremiah says these things; to which he adds: 'And they will drink and vomit and go mad and fall.' So here he named the punishments unmixed wine, which those drink who are worthy of unmixed wine—that is, of unmixed punishment. There are also others who drink a punishment not unmixed but mixed; for 'a cup is in the Lord's hand, full of unmixed wine of mixture; he tipped from this into that; yet its dregs were not emptied out; all the sinners of the earth will drink.' If you also want to see a cup of blessing, which the righteous drink, the one of Wisdom would already suffice, at which she said: 'Drink the wine I mixed for you.' But look with me also at the Savior going up to the Passover into 'a large upper room furnished and ready,' celebrating with the disciples and giving them a cup about which it is written not that he mixed—for Jesus, gladdening the disciples, gladdens with what is unmixed—and says to them: 'Take, drink; this is my blood, poured out for you for forgiveness of sins; do this, as often as you drink, in remembrance of me,' and: 'Amen I say to you, I will not drink it from now until I drink it new with you in the kingdom of God.'

You see the promise being 'the cup of the new covenant'; you see the punishments a cup of unmixed wine, and another kind of punishment a mixed cup—so that for each there is mixed, according to the worth of good practice mixed with base practice, what he will drink. Think with me of those wholly alien to piety and in no way attending to themselves, but living as it happens, drinking the unmixed wine about which we set out the things from Jeremiah; and of those not wholly fallen away and sinners, yet unworthy of the cup 'of the new covenant,' doing sometimes better and sometimes contrary deeds, drinking wine 'of unmixed mixture.' For God 'tipped from this into that'—from what 'this'? I see two cups according to the saying: 'He tipped from this into that; yet its dregs were not emptied out.' Think with me of the cup of your good works in one hand of God; and if you want me to speak more boldly, let the cup of your good works be in the right hand of God, then let the cup of your sins be in the left hand of God.

So when you are about to be punished for sins, since better works have also come to be for you, 'a cup is in the Lord's hand, full of unmixed wine of mixture. And he tipped from this into that'—from the one in the left into the one in the right. For you cannot drink only the cup of goods, as not having done only good works, nor can you drink only the cup of sins, for some good things have been done by you. Therefore 'he tipped from this into that.' According to the proportion of your works wrath and punishment are mixed for you, so that either the punishment may be more watery for you or sharper and more toilsome. For according to the proportion, as I said before, of sins compared with goods, the drink from the cup of wrath somehow grows blunt or does not grow blunt as it is given to each of the sinners.

But if you are wholly fair and good, you say: 'I will take the cup of salvation, and call on the name of the Lord.' So 'every wineskin,' whether fair or wicked, 'will be filled with wine,' and according to the fitness of the wineskin wine will be cast into the wineskin according to the account of the wineskins named here. Oil then is not cast into the wineskins, nor any other liquid matter, but every wineskin must be filled with wine.

title: God fills sinners’ wineskins; scattering as discipline
english: Then he teaches, for those who sinned—as far as the wording goes—then in Jerusalem and in Judea, with what sort of wine God fills these wineskins, the sinners. For it is written: 'If they say to you, “Not knowing, we will not know that every wineskin will be filled with wine,” you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: Look, I fill all who inhabit this land and the kings sitting as sons of David on his throne and the priests.' The one about to punish spares no one. Not because someone was named a prophet, yet has sins, will he not be filled with the threats spoken. Not because someone was named a priest and seemed to have the superiority of a more honored name than the people does God spare him so that he is not punished when he has sinned. And the things written about those people, the apostle says, were written for us, 'upon whom the ends of the ages have come.' If then anyone among these priests also (I mean us elders) or among these Levites standing around the people (I mean the deacons) sins, he will have this punishment—as again there are certain priestly blessings, about which, God granting, not far off but after the examination of the prophetic word we will know when Numbers is read; for something about priests is about to be said there. So 'the priests' and 'the prophets and Judah and all who inhabit Jerusalem,' God says he will fill 'with drunkenness' and scatter 'them, a man and his brother, and their fathers and their sons.' And let us understand these things thus: God gathers the righteous, but scatters the sinners. Therefore also when human beings had not moved from the east, God did not scatter them; but when they moved 'from the east' and 'a man said to his neighbor: Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower whose head will be to heaven,' God says about them: 'Come, let us go down and confuse their tongue there,' and each is confused and scattered to some place of the earth. And the people of Israel, when not sinning, was in Judea; but having sinned is scattered afterward throughout the inhabited world and sown everywhere.
Think something of this kind with me also about all of us.

There is a 'church of firstborn enrolled in heaven,' where is Mount Zion and city of the living God, heavenly Jerusalem. The blessed will be gathered there, that they may be together. But sinners are also punished in this: in not being with one another. I know some in this life who, for punishment, want to hand over to some island and, for torment, the household of someone who grieved the kingdom, scattering—here the wife, here the one son, then elsewhere the other—so that not even in the disaster the mother may enjoy the son, or the brother the brother. Think something of this kind also upon the unjust. You who are a sinner managed by God must taste something more bitter, that being disciplined you may be saved.

And just as you do not punish a household slave or son under your punishment simply wanting to torment him, but that by the pains you may turn him, so also God will discipline those not turned by the word, those not healed, with the pains from sufferings. For discipline he puts around what he puts around according to what is said: 'With toil and scourge you will always be disciplined, Jerusalem.' So that the disciplining pain may grow, those in pain are scattered from one another so that this one and that one may not be together. For the intensity of the pain would be loosened through the comfort of each toward what comes from the other.

title: Why the wicked are scattered from one another
english: But if another cause of being scattered must also be added to the account, I will set this beside it. Bad people being with one another look to the bad things and increase them, just as good people being with good ones consider good things. So the evil counsel is dissolved and divided—having been able to hold with the like—when the wicked are scattered from one another. For this reason God arranges that the worthless not be with one another, perhaps also providing for them, that their wickedness may not grow together but may shrink as it is dissolved. These things because of 'I will scatter them, a man and his brother, and their fathers and their sons together. Says the Lord. I will not long for them and I will not spare and I will not pity from their destruction.'

title: God’s refusal to spare serves the common good
english: Those from the heresies mount upon such sayings and say: Do you see what the craftsman is like? The God of the prophets who says, 'I will not spare and I will not pity from their destruction'—how can this one be good? But if I take as an example a judge who for the common good does not pity and who rightly is not merciful, I will be able from the example to persuade that God, sparing many, does not spare one. And I will also take a physician as example, showing that sparing the whole body he does not spare one member. Let this be set before a judge: to craft peace and arrange what is beneficial for the nation under him. And let someone be brought forward, a murderer fair in appearance and beautiful to see. Let a mother come forward bringing pitiful words to the judge, that her old age may be pitied; let the wife of this one unworthy of pity beg; let children standing around plead about him.

Upon these things what benefits the common? That this one be pitied or not pitied? But if pitied he will return to the same things; if not pitied he himself will die, but the common will be improved. So if God spares the sinner and pities him and has compassion so as not to punish, who will not be worn down? Who of the worthless—those who through fear of punishments stop their sins—will not be worn down and become worse? Such things can also be seen happening in the churches: someone sinned; after the sin he begged about communion. If he is pitied too quickly, the common is worn down. The sin of others grows.

But if by reasoning—not as unmerciful nor as harsh the judge, but as providing also for the one, yet providing more for the many than for the one—he considers the coming damage to the common from the communion of the one and from the forgiveness of his sin, clearly he will cast out the one in order to save the many. Look with me also at a physician, how if he is sparing of cutting what must be cut, if sparing of cauterizing what must be cauterized because of the pains that follow such helps, how the disease grows and becomes worse.

But if he comes more boldly to the cutting and the burning, he will heal through not pitying, through seeming not to have compassion on that one being cauterized and cut. So also God does not manage one human being, but manages the whole world; he administers the things in heaven, the things on earth everywhere. He considers then what benefits the whole world and all that are; as far as possible he also considers what benefits the one—yet not so that the benefit of the one comes at the damage of the world. For this reason eternal fire was also prepared; for this reason Gehenna was also made ready; for this reason there is also an outer darkness—needed not only because of the one punished, but most of all because of the common.

title: The scourging of some trains others
english: But if you want to take Scripture as witness that sinners are punished also for the training of others, even if these at some time are given up as beyond healing, hear Solomon in the Proverbs saying: 'When a pestilent one is scourged, the foolish becomes more shrewd.' He did not say that the one scourged himself will be more shrewd and more prudent through the scourgings, but that the foolish changes from folly to prudence through the scourgings applied to the pestilent one; for this is what the name of shrewdness signifies here. And the foolish changes by seeing others scourged. So it benefits us—if at least we become worthy of salvation through others being punished—the punishment of others. And as Israel's trespass benefited the salvation of the nations, so the punishment of some will benefit the salvation of others. For this reason God, being good, says: 'I will not spare and I will not pity from their destruction.'

title: Hear and give ear; do not exalt yourselves
english: One chapter having been marked off, let us also see what the other teaches us: 'Hear and give ear, and do not exalt yourselves, for the Lord has spoken. Give glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, and before your feet stumble on dark mountains; and you will wait for light, and there is a shadow of death, and they will be placed into darkness.'

'But if you do not hear in a hidden way, your soul will weep from before insult, and your eyes will bring down tears, because the Lord's flock was crushed.' He wants the same people both to hear and to give ear, not content either with their hearing alone or with their giving ear. Therefore he says: 'Hear and give ear.' Then after this he commands them not to exalt themselves, and teaches what must be done. What then is hearing and what is giving ear? Let us understand from the wording itself. 'Give ear'—receive into the ears; and 'hear'—if it is said in distinction from 'give ear'—perhaps is: receive into the mind. And among the things said in the Scriptures some are more ineffable and more mystical, and some are useful at once to those who understand. About the more ineffable I think 'hear' is said; about those useful at once and able without interpretation to benefit the hearer, 'give ear.' So if we examine the whole Scripture we will say, becoming 'approved bankers': hear this, but give ear to that.

Then when we have heard and given ear, he commands us: 'And do not exalt yourselves.' For 'everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.' And the Savior too, in saying, 'Learn from me that I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls,' teaches us not to exalt ourselves. For among the other human evils this sin also is much in us—sometimes exalting ourselves quite irrationally and over what one ought not exalt oneself even in the least, and sometimes with a semblance of reason, that what we exalt ourselves over is reasonable, yet even over that exaltation is not sound.

title: No ground for pride—not even spiritual grounds
english: What I mean will be clear like this: there are some who exalt themselves because they are sons of governors and because they are of a family from great worldly ranks. Such people, exalting themselves over an involuntary and indifferent matter, do not even have a plausible likelihood that what is set beside them for exaltation is reasonable. There are those who exalt themselves because they have authority to kill human beings, and who exalt themselves because they have received what among them is called such a promotion that they cut off human heads. 'The glory' of such people 'is in their shame.' Others exalt themselves over wealth—not the true wealth but the one below; and others exalt themselves, say, over having a fine house or many fields. None of these is worthy of account; one must not exalt oneself over any of these.

But the plausible case about exaltation is when someone exalts himself because he is wise, and exalts himself knowing in himself that already for ten years he has not touched sexual things, or even from childhood has not touched them; and again another exalts himself because he wore bonds concerning Christ. There is a semblance here that suggests that someone reasonably exalts himself—yet even over these, as toward the true account, no one reasonably exalts himself. So there is no reasonable exaltation even over these.

Paul had the material for exaltation through visions, through sights, through wonders and signs, through the toils he toiled for Christ, through the churches he planted, ambitious where Christ was not named to found a church. All these were material for him, if one must speak with the semblance about exaltation, that to some it would have seemed fine for him to exalt himself. But still, since even exaltation over such things is not without danger, the kind Father, as he granted him visions and sights, so also gave him in the portion of a gift 'an angel of Satan to buffet him, that he may not be exalted beyond measure.' And about this he begged the Lord three times that the angel of Satan depart from him—the one given him that he may not exalt himself. And the Lord answered him (for Paul was worthy of the Lord's answer) and said to him: 'My grace is enough for you; for my power is perfected in weakness.'

So one must exalt oneself over nothing; for falling follows exaltation according to 'Before crushing a man's heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled.' So much for 'Hear and give ear, and do not exalt yourselves, for the Lord has spoken.'

title: Give God glory before the darkening
english: Let us also see what he commands us to do after these things: 'Give,' he says, 'glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, before your feet stumble on dark mountains; and you will wait for light.' He wants the one giving 'glory to God' to give 'glory to God' while there is light, as if God's glory cannot be announced when it has grown dark and darkness has come. When then does it grow dark, and when does the darkening not come? 'Work while the light is in you.' 'The light is in' you if you have in you the one who said: 'I am the light of the world.' As long as this rises for you, glorify God; but know that some darkening can come, and one must not remain in this darkening, but before the darkening give glory to God.

title: Who will spare Jerusalem after she killed Jesus?
english: We want to understand the words spoken to Jerusalem with much threat, which run like this: 'Who will spare you, Jerusalem? Or who will look gloomy over you? Or who will turn back to ask after your peace? You have turned away from me, says the Lord.'

'You will go backward, and I will stretch out my hand against you and destroy you, and I will no longer spare you. And I will scatter them in dispersion.' Then: 'I have been made childless. Helplessness has seized me.' I take as an example a certain enemy proved against the one who reigns on earth: that it is not permitted even to give him a share of mercy, lest someone seem to strike against the king who condemned him. And it is not permitted even to pity such a one. Some go further and do not even look gloomy over him, lest by looking gloomy they seem displeased at what the king judged. If you have understood this, look with me at the one condemned by God through his many sins, and see such a person—while there are legions of angels appointed to help human nature—pitied by no one.

For each of the angels, seeing that the one who condemned is God, that the one turned away from is the Creator, and that the nature of the sins is such that the good God was compelled—so to speak—to bring the vote against the sinner, each of those who see does not spare, does not look gloomy, does not pity, does not come back so as to plead concerning peace toward such a one.

So let this Jerusalem (for so it will be said according to the letter) have sinned against my Jesus and done such things that Jesus says about her: 'Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing.'

'Look—your house is left to you.' Let this Jerusalem be left as she has been left. Let the angels who always help Jerusalem—through whom Moses' law also was arranged, 'arranged through angels by the hand of a mediator'—leave Jerusalem and say: her sins have become great; they killed Jesus; they laid hands on the Christ.

As long as the sins were still smaller, we could still plead and intercede about them; we could spare Jerusalem. Who will spare for this? 'If a man sinning sins against a man, they will pray for him; but if he sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?' 'Jerusalem has sinned a sin; therefore she has become a shaking.' And it is said to this one first: 'Who will spare you, Jerusalem? And who will look gloomy over you?' We do not look gloomy over Jerusalem and her disasters and what has happened to that whole people—for by their trespass our salvation has come, to provoke them to jealousy.

Since their trespass has become so great a sin that the Lord's voice is spoken—'Who then will spare you'—I too say to the one who killed my Jesus: 'Who will spare you, Jerusalem? And who will look gloomy over you?'
