title: From Jebus to Jerusalem: the soul that sees peace
english: I move from the letter—though I have already taken the road the word gave—onto each soul already counted worthy to see peace. For after the divine lessons you have become Jerusalem, having formerly been Jebus. History says that one's name was Jebus; then second it changed the name and it became Jerusalem. Children of the Hebrews say Jebus is interpreted 'Trodden.'

So Jebus—the soul trodden by opposing powers—has been changed and has become Jerusalem, Vision of peace. If then, when you changed from Jebus so as to become Jerusalem, you sinned and trampled the Son of God and counted the blood of the new covenant common (as that Jerusalem did, and you too) and are in hard sins, it will be said also about you: 'Who will spare you, Jerusalem? And who will look gloomy over you?'—if you become such as to betray Jesus. Each of us, when we sin—and especially if the sins are greater—sins against Jesus.

And if one is also an apostate, still more does he do to Jesus spiritually what Jerusalem did to him bodily. Therefore: 'How much worse punishment do you think will be deserved by the one who has trampled the Son of God and counted common the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?' If you have trampled the Son of God and insulted the Spirit of grace, who 'will spare you? Who will look gloomy over you? Who will turn back to ask after the things that make for your peace?' The sinner's soul has betrayed the very Son of God who asked after the things that make for your peace. Who can turn back again and plead concerning peace? Knowing then that 'it is impossible to renew again to repentance those who were once enlightened and tasted the heavenly gift and became partakers of the Holy Spirit and tasted the good word of God and powers of the age to come, and fell away, crucifying again in themselves the Son of God and making a spectacle of him,' let us do everything so that it may not also be said about us: 'Who will spare you, Jerusalem? And who will look gloomy over you? Or who will turn back to ask after your peace?'

title: Do not turn back; flee to the mountain
english: And to either interpretation of Jerusalem the next words also fit: 'You have turned away from me, says the Lord. You will go backward.' That you have turned away from the Son of God, and through turning away from the Son of God have turned away from God—what need is there even to say it? And since the Jerusalem in Judea turned away from the Christ—from which all the Jews are to be understood—therefore 'You will go backward.' For there was a time when she did not go backward but forward; but now she goes backward, 'and they turned in their hearts toward Egypt'—clearly so that they might go backward. Concerning what 'You will go backward' is, or what it is to stretch forward to the things ahead, we will set it out like this.

The righteous stretches forward to the things ahead, forgetting the things behind. Clearly the one disposed contrary to the righteous remembers the things behind and does not stretch forward to the things ahead. Remembering the things behind, he disobeys Jesus teaching and saying, 'Let him not turn back to take his cloak'; he disobeys Jesus saying, 'Remember Lot's wife'; he disobeys Jesus saying, 'No one who puts hand to the plow and turns back is fit for the kingdom of God.' And in the law it is written that the angels said to Lot who had gone out from Sodom: 'Do not look back, and do not stand in all the surrounding country; escape to the mountain, lest you be taken along.' And this also has a sense worthy of an angelic spirit: 'Do not look back'—always stretch forward to the things ahead. You have left Sodom; do not turn toward Sodom. You have left wickedness and sin; do not turn back to it, 'and do not stand in all the surrounding country.' Even if you keep the former command that says, 'Do not look back,' it is not enough for you to be saved unless you also hear the second command that says, 'And do not stand in all the surrounding country.' For one who has begun to progress must not stand in the country around Sodom, even if he has crossed Sodom, but having crossed from standing in the surrounding country he must be saved onto the mountain, according to 'Do not look back and do not stand in all the surrounding country; escape to the mountain, lest you be taken along.' If you want not to be taken along with the people of Sodom, never turn back, and do not stand in the country around Sodom, and be nowhere else than on the mountain—for only there is it possible to be saved.
And the mountain is the Lord Jesus, to whom is the glory and the power forever. Amen.

title: Prophets as physicians of souls
english: Physicians of bodies, coming beside the sick and always giving themselves to the therapy of the sick according to the will of the medical art, see dreadful things and touch unpleasant things; on others' misfortunes they reap their own griefs, and their life is always in circumstance. For they are never with the healthy, but always with the wounded, with those who have spreading sores, with those filled with pus, fevers, various diseases. And if someone wants to practice medicine, he will not be irritated nor neglect the will of the art he has taken up when he is with such people as we have said beforehand.

This preface of mine has been spoken because the prophets too are as it were physicians of souls and always spend time where those needing therapy are; for 'the healthy have no need of a physician but those who are badly off.' And what physicians suffer from the undisciplined sick, this the prophets and teachers also suffer from those who do not want to be healed. For from there they are hated, as arranging contrary to the choice of the desire of the sick, as preventing luxury and pleasure for those who even in diseases want not to take what the diseases deserve. So the undisciplined among the sick flee physicians, often also abusing them and speaking ill of them and doing whatever an enemy would do to an enemy.

For these forget that they come as friends, looking to the toilsome character of the regimen, to the toilsome character of the blow from physicians' iron—not to the end after the toil—and hate them as fathers of toils only, and not of toils that bring those being healed toward health.

title: The Word’s strength grows or fails in each soul
english: Let us see whether, the Word himself giving, we can also say something clearer than what has been said toward 'My strength failed among those who curse me.' 'There was the true light, which enlightens every human coming into the world.' 'The true light' is the Son of God, 'which enlightens every human coming into the world.' And whoever is rational shares in the true light, and every human is rational. So of all humans who share in the Word, in some the strength of the Word has grown, and in some it fails.

If you see a passionate and sinful soul, you will see there the strength of the Word failing; but if you see a holy and righteous soul, you will see the strength of the Word bearing fruit day by day, and you will fit what is said about Jesus to the righteous. For not by himself alone 'did Jesus advance in wisdom and stature and grace with God and humans,' but also in each of those who receive the advance in wisdom, stature, and grace, Jesus advances 'in wisdom, stature, and grace with God and humans.' So the Word, the Son of God, who is in the one saying 'Woe is me, mother' and what follows, says that 'My strength failed among those who curse me.'

Whoever curses the Word at once receives the punishment for cursing the Word, for blaming Jesus' teaching; for Jesus' strength fails in such a one, and there is no strength of Word in him. And again from the contrary: if you bless Jesus and accept him, his strength suffers the opposite of what it suffered among those who curse. For as there it failed among those who curse, so here it grows among those who bless.

title: May they be guided; I stood before you in their evils
english: 'May it be, Lord, when they are guided; if I did not stand before you in the time of their evils.' What is 'May it be, Lord'? Let the one able gather such a thing from himself. 'Master Lord, when they are guided'—may the strength that fails among those who curse come to be, when, having repented after speaking ill of me, they turn to the straight way and travel it. 'May it be, Master, when they are guided; if I did not stand before you.' Then he justifies himself about those who speak ill of him saying: 'If I did not stand before you in the time of their evils.' He stood before the Father as 'atonement for our sins' and pleaded about them in that very time of our evils. For he did not stand after the time of our evils, but 'while we were still sinners Christ died for us'—'if I did not stand before you in the time of their evils, in the time of their afflictions, for good against the enemy.' And in the time of their affliction, he says, the one toward the enemy, I stood before you for them. And who is the enemy but 'our adversary the devil,' who afflicted us? And clearly in the time of that enmity against humans our Savior stood before the Father and begged about our captivity, that we might be redeemed and delivered from the enemy. Let the Savior or the prophet have said these things; for the prophet too can have said such things and prayed about the people in 'the time of their evils.'

title: Iron strength; treasures given as plunder to the nations
english: Upon these things God answers toward the people accused by the prophet or by Christ and says these things to him: 'Iron and a bronze covering is your strength'—hard, unyielding, not driven. 'Iron and a bronze covering is your strength'—as if your strength were some cutting and dividing force, not being strength for good. 'And I will give your treasures into plunder, an exchange for all your sins.' Which 'treasures' of those who sin does God give 'into plunder,' and give them 'as exchange for all their sins'? Is it sometime those stored up for themselves on earth? For each of humans stores up; if he is base, on earth, but if noble, in heaven, as we were taught from the Gospel.

Or does he say to that people that because of your sins I am about to give your treasures into plunder? What sorts of treasures of that people were given into plunder? See: one of the treasures was Jeremiah, another treasure Isaiah; Moses too was a treasure. God took these treasures from that people and through Christ, who said: 'The kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits,' gave them to us. So 'I will give because of your sins your treasures into plunder.' And he gave that people's treasures to us; for 'first they were entrusted with the oracles of God,' then after them we were entrusted, the oracles of God having been taken from them and given to us. And we say that 'The kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits' was spoken by the Savior and has been fulfilled—not that the writing was taken from them, but now they no longer have the law and the prophets by not seeing the mind in them.

For they have the books, but how was the kingdom of God taken from them? The mind of the Scriptures was taken from them. No longer is a legal or prophetic interpretation saved among them, because of Christ's sojourn, the 'I said to that people: Hearing you will hear and will not understand, and seeing you will see and will not perceive.'

For the heart of this people was made fat. And what was said by Isaiah has also been fulfilled: that 'The Lord will take away from Judea and from Jerusalem the strong man and the strong woman, giant and warrior man, judge and prophet and diviner and wise master-builder and intelligent hearer.' God took all these away from them and gave them—if at least we receive—to us from the nations. These things because of 'And I will give your treasures into plunder. An exchange for all your sins and in all your borders.'

As if he said: because of your sins that have reached upon all your borders; for there is no border of that people that has not been filled with sin. And how would every border of theirs not be about to be filled with sin—as far as it lay with them—who killed righteousness, if Christ is righteousness; who killed wisdom, if Christ is wisdom; who killed truth, if Christ is truth? For through condemning the Son of God to death they cast off and destroyed all these. And my Lord Jesus, risen from the dead, no longer appeared to those who killed him; for we do not have in the history that he appeared to those who killed him, but only to those who believe did he appear risen from the dead.

title: Enslaved among enemies; do not be long-suffering toward them
english: 'And I will enslave you among all your enemies in the land which you did not know.' That people has been enslaved among the enemies, and has come to be in the land which they did not know. 'For a fire has been kindled from my wrath; it will burn upon you.'

After these things and the words of the threats spoken toward the people, the one who prayed above completes the prayer and joins to what was said beforehand these things: 'You know, Lord; remember me and visit me, and acquit me from those who pursue me—not unto long-suffering.' And let the prophet say these things, pursued by those who were convicted, hated by those who do not make room for the truth; for he became an enemy to those who hear, speaking truly to them. And let our Savior also say the same, who was also pursued by the people and says: 'Not unto long-suffering.' What is 'not unto long-suffering'? You were always long-suffering toward the people upon their sins, but upon the things dared against me do not be long-suffering. And truly God was not long-suffering.

If you examine the times of the passion and of Jerusalem's fall and of the city's demolition, and how God abandoned that people since they killed the Christ, you will see that he no longer used long-suffering toward the people. And if you want, hear: from the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar until the demolition of the temple forty-two years were completed. For some short time had to be granted for repentance, especially because of those from the people who were going to believe from the signs and wonders that would come to be through the apostles.

title: Reproach for your words; share the prophets’ lot
english: 'Know that I received reproach concerning you from those who set aside your words.' Let the prophet, speaking and made nothing of for what he said, be set aside by sinners; for he himself says: 'I continued being mocked.' So he was reproached by those who set aside the words spoken through him by God, and he prays, upon being reproached, to be helped by God saying: 'Know that I received reproach concerning you from those who set aside your words; finish them.' Let the prophet say it, but 'finish them' spoken by the Savior fits better; for a finishing came upon Jerusalem and the people, upon what happened from the people's plot against our Savior.

After these things it is necessary—because the prophets suffered much convicting and ambassadoring the word and taking what was commanded by God—to remind the hearers about their life and their promises and our choice, so that as far as we can, if we want to have rest with the prophets, we may zealously imitate the prophets' works.

What I mean is like this: often in prayers we say: Almighty God, give our portion with the prophets, give our portion with the apostles of your Christ, that we may also be found with Christ himself. And saying these things we do not perceive what we pray; for in effect we say this: grant us to suffer what the prophets suffered, grant us also to be hated as the prophets were hated, give such words for which we will be hated, grant us to fall into as many circumstances as the apostles. For to say 'give me a portion with the prophets' while neither having suffered the prophets' things nor wanting to suffer is unjust. To say 'give me a portion with the apostles' while not wanting from Paul's disposition, speaking truly, to say: 'In toils more abundantly, in blows more abundantly, in prisons beyond measure, in deaths often' and what follows, is most unjust of all. If then we want to come to be with the prophets, look at the prophets' lives—that from convicting, from rebuking, from striking they were judged, examined, condemned. 'They were stoned, they were sawn, they were tested, they died by murder of sword, they went about in sheepskins, in goatskins, lacking, afflicted, mistreated, wandering upon deserts'—when there were many synagogues of Jews; and these were 'wandering upon deserts and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth.' What then is strange if someone wanting to zealously imitate the prophetic life, convicting, striking the one who sins, is spoken ill of, hated, plotted against? Just as also in the present such a thing had to come to be into God's church. The one who was condemned was condemned; so-and-so sitting did such things; there had to be church vindication, and it came to be; the one entrusted with the work did what he ought to have done. That one goes about speaking ill of the one who vindicated the truth. But let us not do this; let us not lend our ears to those who, because they have been cast out, speak ill of the one who cast out or of the one who became a fellow voter. The marvelous apostles, insulted countless times because of the truth, say: 'I am well pleased in weaknesses, in insults and necessities, in persecutions and distresses, for Christ.' Only may I, being insulted, know that I am insulted for no other reason than for Christ; coming into necessities, know that the ground of the necessities is Christ. May I, being abused, know that the pretext of the abuse is no other than that I vindicate the truth and ambassador for what is written, so that according to God's word everything may come to be—for this reason I am blasphemed. So let us all too, as much strength as there is, hasten upon the prophetic life, upon the apostolic life, not fleeing what is burdensome; for if an athlete flees the burdensome of the contest, he will not receive the pleasant of the crown.

title: Your word will become joy; I did not sit with those who play
english: 'And your word will be to me for gladness.' It is not now, but 'it will be'; for upon the present your word is to me for imprisonments, for lawsuits, for affairs, for ill repute, for toils, but the end of these will be gladness. 'And your word will be to me for gladness and joy of my heart, because your name has been called upon me, Lord Almighty.' Even if Christ says it, the Father's name has been called upon him. 'I did not sit in their council of those playing.' If ever the prophet saw the council not of those serious but of those playing, he fled rather gathering than hastened upon a synagogue of those playing. So you must understand a difference between a council of those playing and of those serious. This council is serious and does everything with seriousness and things worthy of seriousness and according to what is said: seriousness is the word, seriousness is the life, and everywhere the council is not of those playing but of those serious.

But when the council, leaving the seriousness about what is necessary, has leisure for the games of this age and games from wickedness, it becomes a council of those playing. So this one says: 'I did not sit in their council of those playing, but I was cautious from before your hand.' Two things being set before me—to sit in a council of those playing and to stumble against you God and not please you, or to rise from a council of those playing and do the things that were dear to you—I chose rather to stand up from the council of those playing and be a friend to you than, doing the contrary, to become an enemy to your blessedness. 'I did not sit in their council of those playing, but I was cautious from before your hand.' And our Savior did not sit 'in their council of those playing,' but stood away from them. And a sign that the Savior has been raised from a council of those playing is his having said: 'Your house is left to you desolate.' For the Word of God has left the Jews' council and made for himself another council and church—the one from the nations.

title: I sat alone and was filled with bitternesses
english: 'I was sitting alone.' And the words are managed here. Whenever there is a multitude of sinners and they do not bear the righteous living righteously, it is not out of place for one fleeing the council of wickedness to imitate the one who said: 'I was sitting alone,' to imitate also Elijah who says: 'Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have dug down your altars, and I alone have been left, and they seek my soul to take it.' And perhaps even if you examine more deeply 'I was sitting alone,' you will find some mind worthy of prophetic depth. Whenever we imitate the life of the many, so as not to be withdrawn and better and exceptional beside the many, I cannot say: 'I was sitting alone,' but: I was sitting with many.

But when my life becomes hard to imitate, so that I become so great that no one is near me in character, in word, in deeds, in wisdom, then I can say—because of being alone such and no one imitating me—'I was sitting alone.'

So it is possible even if you are not an elder and not a bishop and not honored with some church honor to say this, to zealously imitate 'I was sitting alone' and take up a life so as to say: 'I was sitting alone.' 'Because I was filled with bitternesses.' If 'narrow and afflicted is the way,' how does your feast come to be with bitter herbs? For when you feast, it says 'you shall eat unleavened breads upon bitter herbs.' What the word wants saying that the one feasting to God must eat 'unleavened breads upon bitter herbs' must be considered. The apostle interpreted the unleavened breads; the interpretation is not mine; but what follows of the interpretation must necessarily be near the apostolic interpretation.

The apostle interpreted the things about the unleavened breads saying: 'Let us feast not in old leaven nor in leaven of wickedness and evil, but in unleavened breads of sincerity and truth.' It is necessary to give the account about the bitter herbs following upon the unleavened breads being of sincerity and truth. Have sincerity and truth, and bitter herbs will be yours, and you eat with bitter herbs the unleavened breads of sincerity and truth—as Paul. Since he ate the unleavened breads of sincerity and truth, he also ate bitter herbs. How did he eat bitter herbs? Saying 'I have become your enemy speaking truly to you.' How did he eat bitter herbs? 'In toil and labor, and in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, apart from the things besides.'

So the law said: 'You shall eat unleavened breads with bitter herbs'; and it did not say: you shall eat unleavened breads with bitter herbs until you are filled, as upon certain other things it has been said: 'You shall eat and be filled.' But the prophet presses further saying that I did not eat bitterness, but 'I was filled with bitternesses'; as much strength as there was I partook of bitter affairs, so as to partake with the fullest bitter herbs.

title: Why do those who hate me overpower me?
english: 'Why do those who hate me overpower?' He had many affairs; he suffered from those not wanting to hear what is true, and those were more powerful than him here in this age, since the kingdom of God is not from this age but from the better places, as the Savior says: 'If my kingdom were from this world, my servants would have fought, that I not be handed over to the Jews.' So those grieving the prophet overpowered him in this world. That they are strong—look at the martyrs. The judge sits judging and living luxuriously in the lawcourt; the Christian, in whom Christ is being judged, was filled with bitternesses and has been overpowered by the unjust and is condemned.

title: My wound is hard; if you turn I will restore you
english: 'My wound is hard; from where will I be healed?' Those who overpower me strike me, and my wound is hard. Whether he prophesies the Lord's cross (for the cross is a hard wound, as far as it lies with those who crucify him), or whether it is said about all the righteous in whom he receives a hard wound, or even if you hear this upon the prophet (for he too suffered the things written in the prophecy), it admits the same sense according to the wording that says: 'My wound is hard.' 'From where will I be healed?' Even if the Savior says: 'From where will I be healed?' he prophesies the resurrection from the dead after the hard wound; and even if it is taken upon the righteous, after the wounds healing comes again. 'Coming to be it became for me as false water, not having faith'; for the wound does not remain but passes. 'Therefore thus says the Lord: If you turn, I will also restore you.' These things are said again toward each whom God will call to turn toward him. And a mystery seems to me to be announced here in the 'I will restore you.' No one is restored into some place never having been there at all, but restoration is into what is one's own. For example if a limb of mine becomes dislocated, the physician tries to make a restoration of the dislocation.

Whenever someone comes to be outside the fatherland, whether justly or unjustly, and then receives again the power to be in the fatherland according to the laws, he was restored upon his own fatherland. Think the same with me also upon a soldier cast out from his own battle-line and being restored. So here he says toward us who turned away that, if we turn, he will restore us. For the end of the promise is also such, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles in the 'until times of restoration of all things which God spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old' in Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen.

title: Jeremiah the physician sued by the sick
english: That people then was sick; there were various diseases in the people who had called upon God. God sent them physicians, the prophets. One of the physicians was also Jeremiah; he convicted those who were sinning, wanting to turn those doing evil. But those who ought to have listened to what was said accused the prophet and accused him before judges like themselves. And the prophet was always in lawsuits under those who, as far as his prophecy went, were healed, yet through their own disobedience were not being healed. Upon these things he sometimes says: 'And I said: I will not speak nor name the Lord's name. And it became like a burning fire blazing in my bones, and I am undone on every side and cannot bear it.'

And sometimes he says, seeing himself always sued, abused, charged, falsely witnessed against: 'Woe is me, mother, as whom did you bear me?'—he said 'a man' not judging but 'being judged,' and not distinguishing but 'being distinguished throughout all the earth.' And since the sick did not listen to him counseling well and medically, he says: 'I did not benefit.' And since, when he was lending the spiritual silver, those to whom he spoke did not want to listen so as to be benefited from what they heard, he says: 'Nor did anyone owe me, nor did I owe.'

title: Two readings: “I did not benefit” and “I did not owe”
english: But I said these things beforehand, before I interpret 'I did not owe, nor did anyone owe me.' For the writing is double: in most copies 'I did not benefit, nor did anyone benefit me,' but in the most accurate and those agreeing with the Hebrew 'I did not owe, nor did anyone owe me.' So one must both interpret what is commonly current and carried in the churches and not leave unexplained what is from the Hebrew writings. He then proclaimed the word; no one received what was said. As a physician also used up the medicines, the sick being undisciplined and filling their own desires.

Perhaps there is a reciprocal affection through the love of humanity of the one benefited toward the one who benefited, so that the speaker also comes to be benefited, since blessed is the one who speaks into ears that hear.

so that the speaker also comes to be benefited, since blessed is the one who speaks into ears that hear. This benefit then a teacher would be benefited from hearers progressing and improving; he would be benefited by having fruit in them. 'No one benefited me.' For if the speaker must have fruit in them, but the hearer receives wrongly and becomes outside what is said, 'No one at all benefited me' is said—since he did not have this benefit which he would have been benefited from the benefited hearer becoming a cause of progress and blessedness for the one who benefited. And otherwise every one who teaches, in the very teaching, as far as the learner is more intelligent, is benefited into what he teaches, into what he learns. For those who speak become better about the lessons they hand over when the hearers, being intelligent and not simply receiving, but cross-examining and asking and testing the will of what is said. So I did not benefit, nor did anyone at all benefit me.

title: Owing no duty; hearers who refuse the loan
english: And since another interpretation is also necessary because of the more accurate copies having it thus: 'I did not owe, nor did anyone owe me,' we will interpret the saying having it this way too.

The one who indeed gives back to all their dues—fear to the one due fear, tax to the one due tax, tribute to the one due tribute, honor to the one due honor—and giving back to all what is fitting, so as not to owe what is fitting toward some, having honored parents as parents, so to speak, brothers as brothers, sons as sons, bishops as bishops, elders as elders, deacons as deacons, faithful as faithful, catechumens as catechumens—if he gives back all that is fitting, he did not owe. But if he owes doing what is fitting and has not done it, he cannot say: 'I did not owe'; for owing he did not give back. How then will I also interpret 'nor did anyone owe me'? I was lending and wanted to give the spiritual money, but they turned away from what was said and did not present themselves as receptive so as to owe; therefore no one at all owed me. For who received what was said, so that from receiving he might become a debtor of what he heard and be demanded, as a debtor of what was said, for the interest? Better then according to this for the hearer to take logical silver from the speaker and owe than, neither receiving nor taking, not even to owe.
For 'nor did anyone at all owe me' also lies among charges.

title: Jeremiah from childhood; Christ the true prophet to the nations
english: But 'Woe is me, mother, as whom did you bear me, a man judged and distinguished in all the earth?' I do not think fits the other prophets to say as it does Jeremiah. For many of the prophets after some times, after wickedness, after sins, having changed began to prophesy, but Jeremiah prophesies from childhood. And it is possible to give an example from what is written. Isaiah did not hear: 'Before I formed you in the belly I know you, and before you came out from the womb I sanctified you; I have set you a prophet to nations'; nor did he say: 'I do not know how to speak, for I am younger,' but when he saw the vision written in his prophecy, he saw and said: 'Woe is me, wretched am I, for having unclean lips I dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips, and I have seen with my eyes the king, the Lord of hosts,' 'and one of the Seraphim was sent,' he says, 'to me, and touched my lips and said: Look, I have taken away your lawless deeds, and this will cleanse your sins.' So after the sins which he did earlier, later Isaiah became worthy of the Holy Spirit and prophesied. And upon another you would find the like. But Jeremiah is not so; for still from swaddling clothes adorned with the prophetic Spirit he prophesied from childhood.

Or, forcing it, shall we say 'in all the earth' instead of in all Judea? For his prophecy while he was prophesying then did not reach into all the earth. Or perhaps, as upon countless other places we showed Jeremiah to have been spoken in place of our Lord Jesus Christ, so also here we will say. At the beginning I noted: 'Look, I have set you for nations and kingdoms, to root out and to tear down and to destroy and to build and to plant.' Jeremiah did not do this. But Jesus Christ rooted out the kingdoms of the earth's sins and tore down the buildings of wickedness and made, instead of those kingdoms, righteousness and truth to reign in our souls.
So just as those things fitted better to be referred to Christ than to Jeremiah, so I think also many other things and these.

title: The Savior’s “woe” in his humanity
english: First one must speak about the 'woe'—whether because of its ill-sounding character the Savior can say 'woe,' he who also pronounces woes on others. We will set out from agreed sayings, which fit no one but the Savior, how he also wept over Jerusalem; and the voice of one weeping is 'woe.' And it lies in the Gospel that seeing Jerusalem he wept over it and said: 'Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I wanted to gather your children,' and what follows. And clearly these too were spoken by the Savior in the 'Woe that I became as one gathering stubble in harvest and as gleaning in vintage, there being no ear to eat the firstfruits. Woe, soul, that the devout has perished from the earth, and the one who walks upright among humans does not exist. All are judged for bloodshed.'
For he came as one gathering stubble into a harvest in order to reap, and finds many sinners and says: 'Woe that I became as one gathering stubble in harvest.'

He came to vintage fruit of life among humans; he finds many sins in us and for this reason says: 'And as gleaning in vintage, there being no ear to eat the firstfruits.' And elsewhere he says something near these things to the Father: 'What benefit is there in my blood, in my going down into corruption?' What great benefit have I given humans? What worthy of the blood which I poured out for them have they done? 'What benefit is there in my blood, in my going down' from heavens? I have gone down; I came upon the earth; I gave myself over to corruption; I wore a human body; what worthy of them has been set right for humans? 'What benefit is there in my blood, in my going down into corruption? Will dust confess you, or announce your truth?' Such then is also what is said here first by the Savior: 'Woe is me, mother, as whom did you bear me, a man?' Not as God does the Savior say 'Woe is me, mother,' but as human, as in the prophet: 'Woe, soul, that the devout has perished from the earth.'

And the soul was human; for this reason it was also troubled, for this reason it was also deeply grieved. But the Word who was in the beginning with God is not troubled; that one would not say 'woe.' For the Word does not admit death, but it is the human that admitted this, as we have often set out.

title: Christ judged in every martyr
english: 'As whom did you bear me, a man judged and examined in all the earth?' If you see the martyrs everywhere being judged and in each church standing before the judges, you will see how Jesus Christ is judged in each of the martyrs; for he himself is the one judged in those who bear witness to the truth. And you will be persuaded to accept this when you see that he does not say you are in prison when you are in prison, but himself; not you hungry when you are hungry, but himself; not you thirsty, but himself. 'I was in prison and you came to me.

I was hungry and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty and you gave me drink.' So even if a Christian is judged not for something else, not for his own sins, but because he is a Christian, it is Christ who is judged. In all the earth then Christ Jesus is judged; and as often as a Christian is judged, it is Christ who is judged—not only in these lawcourts, but take a Christian to be falsely accused and charged about something: then too Christ is judged unjustly. 'As whom did you bear me, a man judged and examined in all the earth?'

title: Every nation puts the Christian word on trial
english: And still you will understand this way how 'he is judged and examined in all the earth.' Who then does not judge the Christian word? Who among the nations, even simply, does not scrutinize it? Who among the Jews does not speak the things about Christians? Who among the Greeks? Who among the philosophers? Who among private persons? Everywhere Jesus is judged and decided about; and by some he is condemned, by others he is not condemned. If he is not condemned, he is accepted; you open the windows to him, he enters to you; you believe in him, he dines with you.

But if you do not accept when you hear about Christianity, you have done nothing other than condemn Jesus as lying, as leading humans astray, as not speaking truly—through not having believed the word he teaches. 'As whom did you bear me, a man judged and examined in all the earth?' As many as wholly disbelieve condemn him; as many as do not disbelieve but are of two minds about him are examining about him. Jesus suffers two things among humans: by the unbelieving he is condemned, by the double-souled he is examined. If you put on 'the image of the heavenly' after putting off 'the image of the dusty,' you are not earth condemning him, nor are you earth in which he is condemned, nor are you still earth examining him.

title: Strength failed among those who curse me
english: 'My strength failed among those who curse me.'

The apostle says about the Savior that 'he was crucified from weakness.' And the prophet says things near these in 'Lord, who believed our report? And to whom was the Lord's arm revealed? We announced before him as a child, as a root in thirsty ground; we saw him, and he had no form or beauty, but his form was without honor, failing beside the sons of humans. A man being in blow and in toil and knowing how to bear weakness, because his face was turned away from dishonor, he was dishonored and not reckoned. This one bears our lawless deeds and is in pain about us, and we reckoned him to be in toil and in blow and in mistreatment. But he was wounded through our lawless deeds, and has been softened through our sins; the discipline of our peace was upon him; by his bruise we were healed.' So he took up the weakness of our sins and wore us and came to those who curse him, and his strength failed from those who curse him as he came down from heavens. For at once he took up the form of the slave and emptied himself, as the apostle said that 'he emptied himself, taking a slave's form.' So he says: 'My strength failed among those who curse me.'

title: Share the prophets’ rest by their freedom
english: Those who pronounce the prophets blessed, and in blessing them pray to have their share with the prophets, gather from the prophetic words the choice things of their prophecy. They seek to be persuaded that if they live according to those things—even if something harsh meets them in this life when they imitate the prophetic life—they will obtain rest and blessedness with the prophets.

From many places one can gather the prophets’ excellences: their freedom, their taut energy, their watchfulness, their being aroused—that when circumstances came they did not worry, because of that freedom, only that they might rebuke, only that they might turn people back, as prophets do when they speak the word of God with boldness, striking those who sin, even if those being rebuked seemed able to do great things.

But even if one can do this from everywhere, let us see it also from what was read today. The prophet rebuked many, and the prophet spoke to many; for he lived among people who had become sinners, as is clear from the captivity that took place in his times. Having rebuked many, and having been judged by many, he utters such words as these.

title: A man judged and examined in all the earth
english: First let us look from the prophetic word, then also according to the ascent of sense, if it is a prophet’s proclamation. 'Woe is me, mother, as what man did you bear me—a man judged and examined in all the earth?' O mother, as what did you bring me forth—a man judged against all who are on the earth, and examined against all who are on the earth?

For the prophetic task lay before this prophet, and before Isaiah, and before the rest: to teach, to rebuke, and to turn people back. So it lay before this prophet too to examine, to rebuke, to judge—being able both to judge and to be judged with sinners—and to rebuke the sins of the people. And what need is there even to say what those from the people did to them? They stoned one, they sawed another, they killed another 'between the temple and the altar,' and this one, when they were rebuked, they threw into a pit of mire.

And in all of this our Savior has done the same, and better than these, being Lord of prophets. For if he himself was scourged and crucified and handed over by the Jews, or by the teachers of the Jews and the leader of the people, he said: 'Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites.' And he adds upon each: 'Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites.' And he adds upon each 'Woe' and 'therefore' this and that.

And we too, if we are eager for the blessings of the prophets, let us do the same things, so that, because we speak and are judged before many people, we may also say: 'Woe is me, mother, as what man did you bear me—a man judged and examined in all the earth?'

title: The Savior judged with all the earth
english: This prophetic word is more properly referred to the Savior. Grant that the prophet says it; yet he will not say it truly, but perhaps by exaggeration—for he was not examined against all the earth. But if I come to my Savior and Lord, and especially because he will come to judgment, and because of the word 'that you may be justified in your words, and may prevail when you are judged,' I will see that my Savior and Lord is about to stand before the Father, being judged with all of us humans. And he is judged with all humans. I mean: he is judged, he himself is examined, and he stood defending the truth—not as an accuser. 'Woe is me, mother, as what man did you bear me—a man judged and examined in all the earth?' A prophet cannot say 'in all the earth.'

But some who love the Lord are also angry and say that the Savior does not speak this, that the voice is not fitting for the Son of God. Yet one must show that 'Woe is me, mother' is not alien to the Son of God: 'My soul is very sorrowful unto death,' and 'My soul is troubled,' and of the things said in the prophets likewise also here: 'Woe is me, mother, as what man did you bear me—a man judged and examined in all the earth'—or when the gleaning has failed for finding a cluster: 'Woe is me, soul, for the godly one has perished from the earth, and the one who acts uprightly among men does not exist.'

Who says there, 'Woe, for I became as one gathering stubble in harvest'? Does the prophet gather, and want to gather? Does the prophet have a field? But it belongs to no one to gather everything from the harvest and from what was sown, except the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Since therefore there are many falls among the nations, and also sins among us, he says: 'Woe is me, for I became as one gathering stubble.' Let each of us examine himself: is he an ear of grain? Will the Son of God find in him something to glean or to harvest? We will find that some of us are wind-blasted; and if we still have a little in ourselves—two or three grains—our sins are many upon us.

Seeing then also the churches that are so called, filled with sinners, he says: 'Woe, for I became as one gathering stubble in harvest and as a gleaning in vintage.' He came seeking fruit in the vineyard; for each of us is planted, and as a vine 'in a rich place,' and 'he transplanted a vine from Egypt,' and 'I planted you a fruitful vine, wholly true.' He comes, and seeks somehow to glean; he finds some gleaning and short clusters, not flourishing and not many. Which of us has clusters of virtue? Which of us has offspring of God?
translator_notes: κυριώτερον: more properly / more fittingly referred to the Savior.
Klostermann/OCR: κκυρίου → κυρίου; truncated Psalm quotation at section end left unforced.

title: Woe from the Savior’s soul, not from Godhead
english: Let these things be said by me as in a digression upon 'Woe is me, mother.' For it is not alien to the divinity of our Savior, when he beholds the sins of men, that the saying 'Woe is me' should now belong to the Savior—not as God but as man, not as Wisdom but as soul. I set beside it that prophetic word: 'Woe is me, soul, for the godly one has perished from the earth, and the one who acts uprightly among men does not exist.' The blessed soul came upon human life; it took a body for the sake of men. If it sees the sins, it says to the Father: 'What profit is there in my blood, in my going down into corruption? Will dust confess to you?'

But upon us let him not say 'Woe is me,' and upon us let the angels of the heavens not say it. When our Savior says 'Woe is me,' they too will say 'Woe is me'; for they are not better than our Savior, and they also see our stumbles. But blessed are those over whom the angels will not say 'Woe is me,' but rather bless them: for 'there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents rather than over ninety-nine who have no need of repentance.' These things for comfort.

'Woe is me, mother, as what did you bear me?' Whom does he call mother? Among women can he not mean both the soul and Mary? But if someone accepts the word, 'My mother the Holy Spirit recently took me and brought me up to the great mountain Tabor,' and what follows, he can see his mother. 'Woe is me, mother, as what man did you bear me—a man judged and examined in all the earth?' He is judged in all the earth and examined, and he is about to say to each: I have done these things and these, and my economy has worked these things and these, and I endured for your salvation. When the Savior says these things, what shall we do? For he is about to be examined in all the earth.
translator_notes: Gospel of the Hebrews allusion: Holy Spirit as mother (Tabor).

title: I owed nothing, and no one owed me
english: I want to see what follows. It can be referred both to the prophet, according to one narrative, and to the Savior. Let us look also at what comes next: 'I owed nothing, and no one owed me.' 'The ruler of this world comes, and he has nothing in me.' And truly he owed nothing. But each of us is a debtor by sins and a debtor holding a certificate of debt. After his certificate has been wiped out, how many certificates have they made again? 'He who did no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth,' made no certificate of debt.

And what of 'no one owed me'? How shall we explain this of the Savior—'no one owed me'? Even if we have read it this way, we must also know that most copies of the Seventy’s edition do not have it so; later, when we examined the remaining editions as well, we learned that it is a scribal error. And yet—'not even one' to me. So that not even one owed him anything: he forgave all their debts. 'A certain creditor had two debtors; one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. When they had nothing to repay, he forgave them both.'

Do you want to see the two debtors—the one who owed five hundred and the one who owed fifty? From two peoples they have believed in God. The people from the Jews, unbelieving toward Christ, owes the fifty; perhaps we from the nations, who have become more impious than all, owe the five hundred—those of whom it is also said concerning that repentant woman. And yet someone might ask how the five hundred is referred to her. From the word 'and what sort of woman is this who touches him,' to which he said to Simon: 'A certain creditor had two debtors; one owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty,' and what follows.

These things because of 'I owed nothing, and no one owed me,' which it was necessary to set before you. 'I owed nothing, and no one owed me; my strength failed among those who curse me.' Even if he died 'from weakness, yet he lives from the power of God.'
translator_notes: Origen flags οὐδὲ ὠφείλησέ μοι οὐδείς as a graphic error vs most LXX copies.

title: Cursed is the one who hopes in man
english: Then, after many words have gone by, it would indeed have been necessary to speak about each of the things said; but there is no room, with time pressing on. Let us therefore speak to what follows, taking up: 'Cursed is the man who has his hope upon a man.' From those who suppose that the Son of God, the Savior, was merely a man—for they dared, along with many human evils, to say also this, that there is no God who is 'the only-begotten,' 'the firstborn of all creation'—'cursed' is 'the one who has his hope upon a man.' It is clear that those who have their hope upon a man are under a curse.

I would say that I do not have my hope upon a man. Hoping upon Christ Jesus, I do not know a man. Not only do I not know a man, but I know Wisdom, absolute Righteousness, the one through whom 'all things were created' among the authorities. 'Cursed is the man who has his hope upon a man.' Even if the Savior bears witness that what he wore was a man—yet even if he was a man, now he is in no way a man. For 'if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet we know him so no longer,' says the apostle. Through him I am no longer a man, if I follow his words; but he says: 'I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.' Therefore, as he is 'firstborn from the dead,' so he has become firstborn of all humans by changing them toward God.

'Cursed,' then, 'is the man who has his hope upon a man, and will strengthen the flesh of his arm'—whoever ratifies the fleshly things, whoever acquires bodily strength and campaigns according to the flesh. But the holy one is not like that: for 'he does not strengthen the flesh of his arm,' for he 'always' has 'the dying of Jesus in his body,' and he puts to death 'the members that are upon the earth—fornication, uncleanness.' Having put these to death, 'he does not strengthen the flesh of his arm.'

'Cursed is the one who has his hope upon a man.' And at the same time this is said toward those who hope in dignities. So-and-so is my friend; he is a centurion, he is a steward; so-and-so is my friend and is rich and supplies me. Then toward such a person also this is said: 'Cursed is the man who has his hope upon a man.' We hope upon no human being, even if they seem to be our friends; for we do not hope upon them but upon our Lord, who is Christ Jesus, to whom be the glory and the power unto the ages of ages. Amen.
translator_notes: αὐτοδικαιοσύνην: absolute / self-subsistent righteousness (Christ).

title: Fishers of men, then hunters on the mountains
english: It is written in the Gospel according to Matthew that our Savior came beside the sea of Galilee and saw Simon and Andrew his brother casting a net into the sea—for they were fishermen. Then the word says that the Savior, seeing them, said: 'Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men.' And leaving the nets they followed him. And Jesus made them take up fishing for men. And he found two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with their father mending the nets; and he called them too to the same craft, and made them also fishers of men.

And if anyone has perceived those who have from God a grace of speech woven like nets and composed from the holy writings like a casting-net, so that the weave may be thrown around the souls of the hearers, and has perceived this also being done skillfully according to that craft—now our Savior sends fishers of men, having trained them, so that we may be able to come up from the sea and flee its bitter waves.

But those soulless fish, coming up in seines and casting-nets and nets or on hooks, die a death that life does not succeed. But the one caught by Jesus’ fishers and coming up from the sea also dies—yet he dies to the world, dies to sin, and after dying to the world and to sin he is made alive by the word of God and takes up another life. As if you could, by hypothesis, conceive the soul of a fish changing after leaving the fish’s body and becoming something better than a fish—I took an example; let no one take a wrong handle from it—such a thing you will conceive. You have come up from the sea, falling under the nets of Jesus’ disciples; coming out you change the soul; you are no longer a fish lingering in the salt waves of the sea, but at once your soul changes and is transformed and becomes something better and more divine than what it was before.

That it is transformed and changed, hear Paul saying: 'And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as from the Lord who is Spirit.' And this fish, caught by Jesus’ fishers and transformed, leaving its sojourns in the sea, makes its sojourns in mountains, so that it no longer needs fishers who bring it up from the sea, but certain second ones who are called hunters, who hunt from every mountain and from every hill. Therefore go up from the sea yourself, caught in the nets of Jesus’ disciples; change away from the sea, forget it, come to the mountains—the prophets—and to the hills—the righteous—and make your sojourns there, so that afterward, when your time comes, you may be caught by the hunters. Who would these be, if not those appointed to receive the souls that are on the hills, the ones not lying low? And see whether the prophet has not cried these things mystically, setting forth this sense in: 'Behold, I send many fishers, says the Lord, and they will fish them; and after these things I will send many hunters, and they will hunt them upon every mountain and above every hill.'
translator_notes: OCR: ἀνακρκαλυμμένῳ → ἀνακεκαλυμμένῳ; ἐπάων → ἐπάνω; δεῦτε ὀπίσω.
θηρευταί: hunters (Jer 16:16), after the apostolic fishers.

title: Seek the mountains and the cleft of the rock
english: If then you wish to be caught by the hunters, take care not to make your sojourns in the valleys, nor to linger somewhere low, but seek the mountains. Go up to the mountain where Jesus was transformed; go up to the mountain on which Jesus, seeing the crowds, went up, and the disciples followed him, where 'opening his mouth he taught them, saying: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of the heavens,' and the beatitudes that follow these.

And it is not possible for these hunters to catch anyone from elsewhere than from the mountains and the hills and from the clefts of the rocks. For these three things are spoken in the prophet: 'For I will send many hunters, and they will hunt them upon every mountain and upon every hill and from the clefts of the rocks.'

From where then shall I understand the rocks and the clefts in the rocks? I come to Exodus, seeking to find a trace of an account of the clefts of the rocks; I find Moses there wanting to know God, and God promising him and saying: 'Behold, I will set you in a hole of the rock, and you will behold my back parts; but my face will not be seen by you.' If you understand the rock there and see the hole in the rock, seeing, you look upon God through the hole of the rock, and you will also see the many rocks and their clefts. Which then is that rock—the one rock? 'And the rock was Christ'; for 'they drank from a spiritual rock that followed,' and 'he set my feet upon a rock' is said in the ninth and thirtieth Psalm. What is the hole in the rock? If you see Jesus’ sojourn, understanding him wholly as rock, you will see the hole according to his sojourn, through which hole the things after God are contemplated. For such a thing is meant in: 'and you will see my back parts.'
translator_notes: ἐνάτῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ Ψαλμῷ: ninth and thirtieth Psalm (Ps 39 LXX / 40 MT).

title: Many rocks: prophets, apostles, angels
english: But I found one hole of one rock; I move in the word from the hole to the cleft of the rock, and I seek also the many rocks. If I come to the choir—whether of the prophets or of the apostles or even of holy angels who have gone up higher—I say that all who imitate Christ, as he is a rock, become rocks. And just as he has a hole through which God’s back parts are contemplated, in the same way each one, giving a way for God to be understood through the things said by him, makes a hole in himself—or if you wish to name it otherwise, a cleft.

From that hole or cleft you will see through Moses the law, through Isaiah his prophecy, through Jeremiah other words of God. And if an angel also speaks, as he spoke according to what is said in: 'and the angel who speaks in me,' there too I stand upon the angel, and there too I see a rock and a hole of a rock, and I see God in an angelic way.

title: Stay in the clefts; treasure in heaven
english: But I need an example, that I may show how it is possible, having come upon an angel, to see God through an angel. For it is written in Exodus: 'An angel of the Lord appeared to Moses in a flame of fire from a bush.' And Moses sees that the bush burns with fire, and the bush is not consumed. And Scripture did not say, as it said at the beginning that 'an angel appeared,' that thus it remained only an angel of the Lord, but: 'I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.' So God was there being contemplated in the angel, as God is known through the rock and through the hole in it.

You do not know, then, when the hunters are sent. For this reason never come down from the mountains, nor leave the hills, nor be outside the clefts of the rocks; for if you are found outside, it will be said to you as to one who is outside and saying the things of those outside: 'Fool, this night they require your soul from you; and the things you prepared, whose will they be?' And these things will also be said to you if you say: 'I will pull down my storehouses and build greater ones, and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have goods laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, be merry.'

You see the one below the mountains, below the hills, outside the clefts of the rocks, how he wanders even in the judgment about goods, thinking these things are goods. Therefore he says: 'And I will say to my soul: Soul, you have goods laid up for many years.' He has judged the grain and the abundance of earthly things to be goods; for he did not see that the truly good things are not in the cursed earth, but the truly good things are in heaven. He was treasuring on earth, because he thought the things on earth were goods. But if someone turns from treasuring 'on earth,' persuaded by Jesus, to treasuring 'in heaven,' it will not be said to him: 'Fool, this night they require your soul from you,' but the hunters, coming and seeking not the things below but the living things in the mountains, in the hills, those sheltered in the clefts of the rocks, will seize them and lead them away from that hunt—where?—to the rest of the holy and blessed in Christ Jesus.

For 'my eyes,' he says, 'are upon all their ways.' Upon such as these—those who make their sojourns upon the mountains and in the hills and in the clefts of the rocks—God has his eyes upon all the ways. 'And they were not hidden from my face'—such as these; for the base hide from the face of God. Adam, after the transgression, heard 'the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden in the afternoon' and hid; but the holy one is not hidden, but has a heart with boldness toward God according to the holy way of life. For 'if our conscience does not condemn us, we have boldness toward God, and whatever we ask we receive from him.' Adam, then, even if he sinned, did not sin unto an exceedingly harsh sin; for this reason he hid from the face of God. But Cain, more sinful than he and most impious, the brother-killer—what did he do? 'He went out from the face of God.' So that by comparison of evils, to hide from the face of God is the lesser; for even this one hides not brazenly, but ashamed before God. 'They were not hidden,' then, 'from my face.' These who have done these things were once in sins and were fished from the sins that were in the sea.
translator_notes: Pass A overnight crib was truncated; restored from locked Greek before Pass B.

title: First the double repayment, then the fire’s test
english: So that those who were fished and afterward came into the mountains may not suppose that these things have come to them from righteousness, the word reminds not only them but also us of the former sins. Therefore after the benefits it is said: 'And their injustices were not hidden before my eyes.'

What follows is about to put a contest before us. For if we understand it as following, we will take careful thought about the repayment of the sins; and if it seems not to follow what was set out before about those being fished and hunted, even so it throws us into no small contest. For he says: 'And I will repay first double their injustices and their sins, with which they profaned my land in the carcasses of the abominations and by their lawless deeds with which they filled my inheritance.' Whether some, not understanding, removed the 'first' from what is written, or the Seventy managed to remove it, God would know. But we, comparing with the remaining editions, found it lying there: 'And I will repay first double their injustices,' so that it may be shown that even if through their second works they were worthy of blessedness, since they are humans and have come to be in sins, they must first receive their sins.

And see whether the word is not true. Who will not receive the sins—except the one who, after believing and receiving forgiveness of sins (so as to hear Jesus say: 'Your sins are forgiven you'), no longer sins? But if after the forgiveness of sins and the economy of the washing of regeneration we sin—as we the many do, who have not been perfected like the apostles—and after sinning, and while sinning, also do some things that are due, what awaits us must be considered. If we leave life holding sins and also holding brave deeds, will we be saved through the brave deeds and released concerning the things we sinned in knowledge? Or will we be punished through the sins and nowhere receive a wage for the brave deeds? But neither the one—I mean receiving the worse and not receiving the better—is according to the just God, nor the other—I mean receiving the better and not receiving the worse—is according to the just God, who wants to cleanse and cut out the wickedness.

For grant that you have built, after the foundation Christ Jesus whom you were taught, not only gold and silver and precious stone—if indeed you have gold, much gold or little; grant that you have silver, precious stone; but not only these, I say—grant that you also have wood and hay and straw. What do you wish to happen to you after departure? Either to enter into the holy things with your wood and with your hay and straw, so as to defile the kingdom of God? Or again do you wish to remain because of the hay, the wood, the straw in the fire and receive nothing for the gold and silver and precious stone? This too is not reasonable.
translator_notes: ἀνδραγαθήματα: brave / virtuous deeds (overnight crib misread as marriages).
πρῶτον in Jer 16:18: Origen prefers editions that keep 'first'.

title: First the consuming fire, then the goods
english: What then? First it follows that, because of the wood, one receive the fire that consumes the wood and the grass and the straw. For our God is said—by those able to understand—to be by substance a consuming fire. And the prophet was silent about what it consumes when he said: 'Our God is a consuming fire,' but he left it for us to understand. Because he said 'God is a consuming fire,' there is something that is consumed. What then is consumed? He does not consume that which is according to the image and likeness; he does not consume his own creature, but the grass built upon it, the wood built upon it, the straw built upon it.

The place was extremely hard to narrate. There were promises, and after the promises he says: 'And I will repay first double their injustices.' The 'first' is necessarily set beside it; for first the things of injustice are repaid, then the things of righteousness, for God does not repay in reverse. If he first repaid the goods so that we might receive the goods, and now repaid the evils, the goods would have to stop so that we might receive the evils. But first we will receive the evils, and after these the goods, so that through the disappearance of the evils the punishment of those who suffered may come to an end, and after these he may repay the goods.

Therefore you will find in the holy writings God saying first the things that seem more gloomy and after these the better: 'I will kill and make alive; I will strike, and I will heal.' 'He himself causes pain and again restores; he struck, and his hands healed.' Upon these things the one who understands and is piously set toward what is said can say: 'Lord, who will sojourn in your tent? Or who will encamp on your holy mountain? Walking blameless and working righteousness, speaking truth in his heart; who has not dealt deceitfully with his tongue, and has not done evil to his neighbor, and has not taken up a reproach against those nearest him.' (But we reproach even those who repent and turn back, though Scripture says: 'Do not reproach a man turning away from sin.') 'He has not taken up a reproach against those nearest him; an evildoer is despised before him, but he honors those who fear the Lord.' We will receive our sins.
translator_notes: Pass A overnight crib truncated after 'difficult to recount'; restored from locked Greek.
Section-end Greek is OCR-frayed; closing clause kept within the Psalm/reproach thread.

title: Why the sins are repaid double
english: But someone among the hearers will say: Narrate also the 'double.' Grant that I first receive the sins, so that when I have received the sins, afterward what was said by the apostle may be fulfilled: 'If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire'—why then do I receive the sins 'double'? But it must be said that 'the servant who knew his master’s will and did not do according to his will will be beaten' not with few blows but with 'many.' Therefore it is right that those from the nations who sin receive their sins simply, but that we receive our stumbles double. For 'if we sin willingly after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a fearful expectation of judgment, and a zeal of fire about to eat the adversaries.'

The things about those who will be fished and hunted and will first receive double their sins were prophesied. After these things the calling of the nations is prophesied more clearly—not of those being called but of those already called, and not of those who do not know what they will confess and what they will give thanks for, but of those who have already learned. For in the former things we were learning that they were called, were fished, were hunted; what they will suffer is in the latter things. Let us see what he prophesies about us who are already learning to pray—or rather who have learned.

title: Nations from the end of the earth
english: 'Lord, my strength and my help and my refuge in a day of evils; to you nations will come from the end of the earth and will say: How false were the idols our fathers acquired, and there is no profit in them.' From the end of the earth the nations came to God, and the nations have said: 'How false were the idols our fathers acquired, and there is no profit in them.'

How 'from the end of the earth'? There are some who are first of the earth, and there are some who are last of the earth. Who are first? 'The wise of the world' are first of the earth—not simply first, but 'the wise of the world, the well-born,' the rich, those in office. Who are last? 'God chose the foolish things of the world, the ignoble, the despised, the things that are not.' Therefore 'nations will come from the end of the earth,' as if he said: from the last of the humans upon the earth, from the foolish, from the ignoble, from the despised, 'and they will say: How false were the idols our fathers acquired, and there is no profit in them.' Not that there are some true idols, against which the false are spoken by contrast, but idols which by nature are false—'and there is no profit in them.'

title: Making gods from doctrines of the soul
english: 'If a man will make gods for himself.' Not only from statues do men make gods for themselves, but you will also find them making gods for themselves from moldings of the mind. For as many as can mold another god and another world-making besides the one written up by the Spirit—a management of the world besides the true world—all these have made gods for themselves and have worshiped the works of their hands. Consider, for example, among the Greeks those who generated doctrines of this philosophy or that, or among the heresies those who first generated doctrines: these made idols for themselves and moldings of the soul, and turning they worshiped the works of their hands, accepting their own moldings as truth.

Therefore the word, refuting all who make gods for themselves both sensibly and intelligibly, says: 'If a man will make gods for himself—and these are not gods? For this reason I will show them my hand at this time, and I will make known to them also my power.' At what time, if not this one—pointing to the time of the Lord’s presence? 'And they will know,' he says, 'that my name is Lord.'
translator_notes: ἀναπλάσματα: moldings / fabrications of the soul (doctrinal idols).

title: Judah’s sin engraved on the heart
english: Then there is another prophecy, which somehow we did not find among the Seventy, but we found in the remaining editions—clearly lying in the Hebrew—and it is filled with most necessary matters that can, if we pay attention, turn our soul back. The words run thus: 'The sin of Judah is written with an iron pen, engraved with an adamant point upon the breast of their heart.'

It is easier to give oneself over and say: These things are written about the Jews, that their sin 'is written.' But if you see, as we have often shown, Judah spoken tropically as Christ, perhaps 'the sin of Judah' is ours—of those who believe upon Christ who is from the tribe of Judah. And if you can also hear it more mystically another way, perhaps it prophesies about Judas who handed him over, so that the prophecy about him says: 'The sin of Judah is written with an iron pen, engraved with an adamant point upon the breast of the heart.' But again 'their' does not follow for that one. Perhaps then he was speaking upon us: if we become sinners, these prophesied things reach us.

We have sinned, and our sin is not written outside us, but in our heart, and it is written 'with an iron pen, with an adamant point.' That the sins we commit are inscribed into us by the sinning, the matter itself will show. I did not know this deed or this sin in myself; having done it I have its imprint, and as it were the imprint of my committed sin has been written in my soul. And if my sin had been written with ink, I would have wiped it away; but now it is written 'with an iron pen,' written 'with an adamant point,' written 'upon the breast of our heart,' so that I may come to the place of teaching and the prophecy that says may be fulfilled: 'Nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, and nothing covered that will not be revealed.' My breast was stripped bare, and the heart holding the written letters of the sin—'with the pen upon my breast and in my heart the imprints of my sins.' For 'nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest.'
From these things may the God of all deliver us, that we may rise into the glory that is in Christ, to whom be the glory and the power unto the ages. Amen.
translator_notes: Jer 17:1 not in Origen’s LXX; he cites the remaining editions / Hebrew.
Closing doxology follows the locked Greek end of the slice.

title: The partridge: crafty, unclean, not the Savior
english: We have come upon the much-discussed question, to see what the partridge is, concerning which Scripture now says: 'A partridge called; it gathered what it did not bear, making its wealth not with judgment. In the middle of its days they will abandon it, and at its end it will be a fool.'

From the account of the natures of animals we must take up what has been recorded about the partridge, so that knowing the things about the animal we may know whether the partridge now spoken of must be ranked upon a better or upon a worse. It is said to be a most ill-natured animal, and deceitful, and thoroughly crafty, wanting to deceive those who hunt it, and often rolling about the feet of the hunter so as to distract him—as if the animal were near—so that he may not come upon the nest. And whenever it judges that it has distracted the hunter and the nestlings have fled, then it too flies away. And the animal is utterly unclean, so that the males fight one another over mating and male mounts male.

If then this animal is ill-natured and unclean and thoroughly crafty and deceitful, it is clear that to rank it upon a better and to say it can be referred to the Savior appears impious. Therefore we must see, if we wish to interpret it of the opposing one, whether the whole interpretation follows for us.
translator_notes: πέρδιξ / perdix: partridge (Jer 17:11 LXX), here of the opposing power.

title: The partridge gathers another’s creatures
english: Let us begin from: 'A partridge called; it gathered what it did not bear.' Therefore the devil does not gather his own creatures; he does not gather what he begot; but when he calls, he gathers another’s creatures and makes them his own. A partridge called through Valentinus; a partridge called through Marcion; it called through Basilides, through all the heterodox. For none of those could speak the voice of Jesus: 'My sheep will hear my voice.' But the voice of Jesus is in Paul and Peter; therefore Paul said: 'Do you seek a proof of Christ who speaks in me?'

But the voice of the partridge that gathered what it did not bear is in those who lead astray and deceive, through their simplicity and lack of preparation, the simpler among the believers. Therefore 'a partridge called; it gathered what it did not bear, making its wealth not with judgment.' The partridge grew rich. See how many myriads are his; many have become the partridge’s—of the opposing power. And he made his wealth not caring about judgment and not having judgment, but acting without judgment. Therefore it is said that the partridge is 'making its wealth not with judgment.' But my Savior makes his wealth with judgment, and his wealth is judged and chosen.

title: In the middle of his days we abandoned him
english: 'And in the middle of his days they will abandon him.' We all who once came under the calling partridge—for he called not only through those named before, but also through all who simply deceive and, as if unto piety, summon godlessness unto doctrines contrary to the truth—but 'in the middle of his days' we have abandoned him. For all his days are the days of this age; but since Christ Jesus drew us out of the present evil age, therefore 'in the middle of his days' we have abandoned him.

'And at his end he will be a fool.' For when was he wise, that at his end he should become a fool? But we will say that he was wise; for 'the serpent was the wisest of all the beasts of the earth which the Lord God made.' Wise he was according to what is said in Isaiah: 'For I will bring upon the great mind, the ruler of the Assyrians. For he said: By strength I will do it, and by wisdom...'
translator_notes: Greek of Homily 17 breaks mid-Isaiah citation; Latin witness resumes in §17.4.

title: His end a fool; Christ the throne of glory
english: 'If anyone among you seems to himself to be wise in this age, let him become a fool.' Attend: he did not only cry, 'Be a fool and senseless,' but 'that you may become wise.' If therefore there is a blameworthy wisdom, according to which 'the sons of this age are wiser than the sons of light in this generation,' God is good, who overturns diversities by contraries, that what was said may be fulfilled: 'his end will be a fool.'

When will his end be a fool? It is necessary that Christ 'reign until God puts all his enemies under his feet'; and when he has subjected all things to him, 'the last enemy, death, will be destroyed.' When death has been destroyed, then will be the utmost of the partridge, and his end will become a fool. These things about the partridge.

The beginning of the second chapter that was read is this: 'A throne of glory exalted from the beginning is the place of our sanctification; our endurance, the endurance of Israel. Lord, all who have forsaken you shall be confounded; departing, they shall be written upon the earth, because they have forsaken the fountain of life, the Lord.' Isaiah the blessed prophet, seeing the Lord and his kingdom, said: 'I saw the Lord of hosts sitting upon a throne high and lifted up.' Jeremiah also saw how God reigns; therefore glorifying him he says: 'A throne of glory exalted from the beginning is the place of our sanctification.'

Whether you wish to understand these things of Christ, you will not err; or of the Father, you will not think impiously: for the Savior is a throne of glory high and from the beginning. 'Throne of glory,' because his kingdom is high; and 'our sanctification' is Christ; for 'he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one.' 'Endurance of Israel': just as the Savior is absolute righteousness, absolute truth, absolute sanctification, so also absolute endurance. And it is not possible to be righteous apart from Christ, nor holy apart from him, nor to endure without having Christ. For he himself is the endurance of Israel. And if you refer it to God, not even so do you go wrong.
translator_notes: §17.4 preserved mainly in Jerome’s Latin; Greek resumes mid-thought on sanctification/endurance.

title: Heal me, Lord—you alone are my boast
english: Then again a prayer stands thus: 'Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for you are my boast.' They say to me: 'Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come.' And I answer: I did not tire out following behind you, and I did not long for a day of man—you know.

Only the physician who came for the sick, who says, 'The strong have no need of a physician, but those who are badly off,' can hear from every soul that wants healing: 'Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed.' If some other promises a medicine of souls, you cannot truthfully address him with that prayer. The woman with the flow of blood spent everything on physicians and was healed by none of them; it was not fitting to say to any of them, 'Heal me, Lord,' but only to the one whose garment-fringe is enough to touch.
