So I say to him: 'Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed.' If you heal, healing follows from you, and I am saved. Whoever else would save me does not save me; only if Christ saves is salvation true. 'A horse is a lie for salvation,' and everything besides God is a lie for salvation. Therefore: 'Save me, Lord, and I shall be saved'—if I can also renounce every boast and say, 'you are my boast,' fulfilling: 'Let the wise not boast in wisdom, nor the strong in strength, nor the rich in riches, but let the one who boasts boast in this: understanding and knowing that I am the Lord.' Blessed is the one who has put away every lower boast—birth, beauty, body, wealth, glory—and is satisfied with the one boast: 'you are my boast.'

title: Following without weariness; desire God’s day
english: 'Behold, they say to me: Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come. But I did not grow weary following after you.' Jesus says to you: 'Take up your cross and follow me,' and 'Leave all things and follow me,' and 'Whoever does not leave father and mother and follow after me is not worthy to be my disciple.' If then you become such that you always follow Jesus, you will also follow, and as long as you follow you will not grow weary; for 'there will be no toil in Jacob, nor will pain be seen in Israel.' There is no labor for the one following Jesus; the very following takes away the labor.

Therefore he himself says, so that we may no longer grow weary—having grown weary before we began to follow him: 'Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.' If then, laboring, we come to him and follow him, we will say: 'But I did not grow weary following after you.'

And it is consequent for us to say also: 'I did not desire a human day.' There is a day of a human, and there is a day of God. Let each of us desire the day of the resurrection of the holy ones, not that day concerning which it is written: 'Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord; and this is darkness and not light.' Who is the one who says: 'And I did not desire a human day'? The clarity of the word will convict us that we have desired a human day. Often when we have fallen sick and come into a fantasy of death, at the departure we beg the brothers who watch over us and say: Ask for me a leave, ask for me to remain in life. Saying these things we do not desire a holy day of God, but a human day. Therefore putting away love of the body and the desire for a human day, let us seek to see that day in which we will obtain the blessedness in Christ Jesus, to whom be the glory and the power unto the ages. Amen.
translator_notes: φιλοσωμία (OCR φιλοςωία): love of the body / bodily life.

title: Clay that can be remade; earthenware that cannot
english: Two visions of Jeremiah in succession have been read. The former holds what concerns the clay vessel in the potter’s hand, which after being shattered still admits setting right—for it can be reshaped. The other vision holds what concerns the earthen jar: once that is broken, there is no healing. While it was clay, if it broke—even if already formed—because it was clay it could become a second lump again and be made a second time. But when after clay it has already become earthenware and has been hardened by fire, then after the earthenware is shattered healing cannot come to it.

What then do these things want? First let us take them in an overview; then, if it is granted, let us examine them according to the letter. As long as we are in this life we are being formed—so I name it because of our clay vessel—by a potter’s work, and we are formed either according to wickedness or according to virtue. Yet we are formed so as to admit even that our wickedness be shattered, that a better new creation may come to be, and that our progress after its formation be dissolved again into a clay vessel.

But whenever after the present age we have come, near the end of life, and then have been fired either by the fire of the evil one’s flaming darts—whatever we become—or by the divine fire (since 'our God is a consuming fire'), if we become by this or that fire whatever we become, and if we are shattered—whether after becoming good vessels we were shattered and have perished, or after becoming worthless vessels—we are not remade, nor does our construction admit improvement. For this reason, as long as we are here, being as it were in the potter’s hand, even if the vessel falls from his hands, it admits healing and being remade. Let these things be said somewhat more readily, before we examine what remains, about the two kinds of vessels: the clay not yet fired into earthenware, and the second already become earthenware.
translator_notes: πήλινον vs ὀστράκινον: clay (still remoldable) vs fired earthenware.

title: Go down to the potter’s house
english: Let us look from the wording itself at what is said about the clay vessel in the potter’s hand, and how the Word in the prophet—the Lord who prophesies in him—also gives not small starting-points for interpreting the things about the formation in the potter’s hand. 'The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Arise and go down into the house of the potter.' Jeremiah is above; he has gone up beyond the clay vessels. Below are the clay vessels, and the nature that administers the clay vessels, going down with those administered, is below. Therefore the word spoken to Jeremiah from the Lord says to him: 'Arise and go down into the house of the potter, and there you will hear my words.'

To Moses it is said: 'Go up into the mountain and hear'; to Jeremiah: 'Go down into the house of the potter and hear.' For each of those who hear a word is either taught about the things higher up or learns about the things lower down. If I am taught the lower things, I go down by the word in order to see the lower things; if I learn the higher things, I go up by the word upon the higher things in order to behold what is there.

And that all of you may, as far as you can, follow what is said, I will use examples also from Scripture, and with the example I will also set out clarity that helps the interpretation given. 'In the name of Jesus every knee will bow of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.' And there is a wisdom about each of these: a wisdom about the heavenly things, how the heavenly things are arranged; a wisdom about the under-earth things, since there is a wisdom of God also about the arrangement of the under-earth things; likewise also about the things on earth. If I am about to make room for the wisdom about the heavenly things, I go up upon the heavenly things, as Moses went up upon the peak of the mountain, that the voice from heaven might become audible to him according to what is written. For he was about to be taught heavenly services; for a shadow and pattern of heavenly mysteries is in the laws of service that have been written up, as the apostle taught when he said: 'who serve a pattern and shadow of the heavenly things.'

title: The vessel fell by itself from his hands
english: So the prophet goes down into the potter’s house and narrates what he saw, saying: 'And behold, he was doing work upon his hands, and the vessel which he was making in the clay in his hands fell apart; and again he made it another vessel, as it was pleasing before him to make.' But I do not know what the prophet saw when he came to be beside the potter. For he saw the potter working; the vessel that had come to be was clay; the vessel fell apart. What exactly did he not say? He did not say: he let the vessel go from his hand—nor did he set the cause upon the potter. But since the word is about ensouled vessels, which fall apart from themselves, therefore it has been said: 'the vessel fell apart from his hands.'

Attend then also to yourself, lest while you are in the potter’s hands and still being molded you fall apart from his hands from yourself. For 'no one snatches out of his hands,' according to what is said in the Gospel according to John. Yet it is not written that as no one snatches, so no one falls apart from his hands; for the self-determining power is free. And I say: no one will snatch out of the shepherd’s hand; no one can take us out of the hand of God; but we ourselves, by neglecting, can fall apart from his hands.
translator_notes: διέπεσε: fell apart / slipped away—Origen stresses free fall, not divine dropping.

title: Spring and well; resurrection of the clay
english: 'And a word of the Lord came to me, saying: If as the potter I will not be able to do to you, house of Israel? says the Lord.' Each according to power understands what is written—one more on the surface, as taking the sense from them as from a spring on a plain; another more deeply, as drawing up from a well. And both can be benefited, since the same thing is a spring to the one and a well to the other. The Gospel bears witness when it narrates the things about the Samaritan woman; for there the same is named 'spring' and 'well,' and by turns it is sometimes called spring and sometimes well. Let the one who can consider, that he may know that the same thing in substance is a spring to the surface-minded and a well to the deeper.

This is a preface for me of the narration about to come, because of the clay vessel that fell apart from the potter’s hand and was molded again. Some considered these things more simply and understood. I will set their account and narration before you; after these things, if we have something deeper, we will narrate that too. Here, they say, the things about the resurrection can be shown. For if the clay vessel fell apart from the potter’s hands and from the same matter of the same clay he makes 'it another vessel as it was pleasing before him,' the potter God of our bodies, the craftsman of our construction, when this falls apart and is crushed for whatever cause, can take it up again and renew it and make it a more beautiful and better 'other vessel as it was pleasing before him to make.' Let this narration also have its grace.

title: Two nations in the potter’s hands
english: But let us hear the Lord himself narrating and saying: 'If as the potter I will not be able to do to you, house of Israel? says the Lord. Behold, as the clay of the potter, so you are in my hands. At the end I will speak upon a nation and a kingdom to lift them away and to destroy; and that nation will turn from their evils of which I spoke toward it, and I will repent of the evils which I planned to do to them. And at the end I will speak upon a nation and a kingdom to be built up and planted; and they will do the evil things before me so as not to hear my voice, and I will repent concerning the goods which I spoke to do to them, says the Lord.'

We see this according to the house of the potter referred not to some one by one, but to two nations; for beginning he says that he is about to speak about nations, that he may suggest something to those able to hear unspeakable mysteries: 'At the end I will speak upon a nation.' Seek also the end and the former nation, upon which he speaks the things of destruction because of their sins; and having spoken the things of destruction because of the sins, he no less promises that if they repent, he will repent concerning the evils which he spoke to do to them. And again he speaks upon another, second nation 'to be built up and to be planted'—a whole nation; and since this nation being built and planted has a good promise, yet can sin, he says after speaking these things, if they stand away from the good works: 'I will repent concerning the goods which I spoke to do to them.'

What then are the two nations—the former named which the word threatens, and the second to which it promises? Yet it threatens so that, if it should repent, he may not do the things of the threat. It promises so that, if it should fall away and the second nation should not become worthy of the promises, it may not attain them. Concerning two nations especially the whole economy of God toward humans in the world is set forth. That former nation was Israel; this second is from the sojourn of Christ. God threatened the former with what he threatened, and we see the things of the threat upon the former nation: it has come to be in captivity, it has been cast down.

And it is possible for this nation also, having sinned, that the same things happen which were said to those because of sins, and they will suffer if they do not repent. Search all Scripture, and you will find most things said about these two nations. God chose the fathers, gave them a promise, led a people out from the race of the fathers from Egypt, was long-suffering upon them when they sinned, disciplined them as a father, led them in, gave them a land of promise, sent them prophets at times, disciplined and turned them from their sins. He was always long-suffering, sending those who heal, until the chief physician should come—the prophet differing from prophets, the physician differing from physicians. When this one had come they betrayed him and killed him, saying 'Away, away with such a one from the earth; crucify, crucify him.' At once a visitation came upon the nation; the place where my Jesus was crucified was made desolate; God chose another nation.

'The harvest, you see how great it is, even if the workers are few.' And otherwise God manages that the net always be cast upon the sea of this life, and fishes of all kinds are gathered; he sends 'the many fishers'; he sends 'the many hunters'; they hunt from 'every mountain,' they hunt from 'every hill.' See how much economy there is about the salvation of the nations. 'See then the kindness and the severity of God: upon' the former nation that also fell 'severity; but upon you' the second nation promises and 'kindness, if you continue in the kindness; since you too will be cut off.' For the axe was not then only lying toward the root of the trees. The axe is ready to come again; 'and the axe lies toward the root of the trees,' my Jesus was saying then, prophesying about Israel beside whom the axe was. He himself was the axe of the unfruitful tree and said: 'Already the axe lies toward the root of the trees.' As many trees as were there not making fruit were cut out and cast into the fire and have been punished.

But now another farm has come to be analogous to the former, concerning which it has been said: 'Leading them in, plant them into the mountain of your inheritance, into your prepared dwelling.' God led his nation into the mountain of his inheritance. I seek the mountain not as Jews do in soulless materials. The mountain is Christ. In this we were planted; upon him we were kept. See then, even if he is long-suffering, lest the master of the house come and say: 'Already three years I come upon this fig tree and it has not borne fruit; cut it out; why does it also make the ground idle?' For the one who comes upon a synagogue and does not bear fruit makes idle the good ground—Christ, the mystery of the church.
translator_notes: μετανοήσω of God: repent / relent (Jer 18:8–10); kept as Origen’s wording.

title: God “repents” as one speaking to children
english: 'At the end I will speak upon a nation or also upon a kingdom.' It will seem that the end has been spoken simply. But such a thing has been said. In 'I will speak upon a nation or kingdom,' the end is of this sort: 'I will tear down' is said as the end to the former nation; to the second: 'I will rebuild you.' And again 'I will uproot' is said to the former, and 'I will plant' to the second. Since then the end has been spoken, must the end come to be? God who does not repent is said according to Scripture to repent. And let us attend to the wording, that if we can make a defense how these things are said, we may accept the word.

'At the end I will speak,' he says, 'upon a nation or upon a kingdom to lift them away and destroy; and if that nation turns from their evils of which I spoke upon it, I will also repent concerning the evils which I planned to do to them. And at the end I will speak upon a nation or upon a kingdom to be built up and planted; and they will do the evil things before me so as not to hear my voice, and I will repent concerning the goods which I spoke to do to them.' Concerning the repentance of God we are required to make a defense; for it seems blameworthy and unworthy not only of God but even of the wise man to repent. For I do not conceive a wise man repenting; but the one who repents, as far as the custom of the word goes, repents over not having planned well. But God, being foreknower of the things to come, cannot have planned badly and for that reason repent. How then did Scripture introduce him saying 'I will repent'—and in the Kingdoms: 'I have regretted that I anointed Saul as king,' and generally: 'and repenting over the evils'?

But see what we are taught generally about God. On the one hand: 'God is not as a man to be deceived, nor as a son of man to be threatened,' and we learn that God is not as a man; and through another wording that God is as a man, when his economy is intertwined with human affairs. For 'of his greatness there will be no end,' and countless other things from the holy writings fit 'God is not as a man.' But when the divine economy is intertwined with human affairs, it bears the human mind and manner and wording.

And just as we, if we converse with a two-year-old child, babble because of the child—for keeping the dignity of perfect adult age without coming down to their dialect we cannot make the children understand—conceive something such also about God, whenever he manages the race of humans, and especially those still infants. See how we perfect men also change the names toward infants. Are we then imperfect? Or is it granted that one speaking to a child by accommodation speak a child’s dialect? And God indeed speaks to children; 'Behold,' says the Savior also, 'I and the children whom God has given me.' So then conceive also the Scripture saying: 'The Lord your God bore your manners, as if a man should bear the manners of his son.' Since then we repent, whenever God converses with us who repent he says: I repent; and threatening us he does not pretend to be a foreknower, but as speaking to infants he threatens.
translator_notes: ἐτροποφόρησεν: bore / wore your manners (Hebraism Origen explains).

title: I am fashioning evils—make them fall from my hand
english: Next after the word about the two nations—the former to which the threat is given, and the second to which the promise is given—he says (clearly he spoke to the former): 'And now I said to men of Judah and to those inhabiting Jerusalem: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I fashion evils upon you.' Because these things which I fashion upon you are in my hand, they can fall away. Make these things fall away from my hand, that I may change the evils which I fashion upon you and do goods.

You would not find: 'Behold, I fashion goods upon you' and the things said next according to their proportion, that after this he might show that the goods which he fashions he releases from the hands, in order to make them evils. But he fashions evils according to the example said, and fashioning evils he manages (apart from the interpretation already given into 'it fell from my hands'), so that if it falls, even the end of the evils being fashioned—I do not know of what sort it may become.

title: Do not walk behind your turnings-away
english: 'Let each turn from his evil way, and make your practices better.' Sometimes the more simple say: Blessed are the older humans, because they heard the Lord through the prophet saying: 'And the Lord spoke to them.' And now the Lord says also to us through the things written: 'Let each turn from his evil way'; the Lord himself converses with you saying: 'And make your practices better.'

But these answered to whom the exhortative words about repentance were spoken, and let us see what they answered, that we too may not answer such things. What then answering do they say? 'We will take courage, that we will go behind our turnings-away, and each of us will do the pleasing things of his evil heart.' And if you do not say it in words, but your life is such as to sin, you also say by force through the evil deeds after the exhortative words: 'We will take courage…'

And what is 'we will go behind our turnings-away'? Those who began to put the hand to the plow and those being taught turned away from the base things. Whenever then someone putting the hand to the plow turns to the things behind, he will go 'behind his turnings-away'; for he will go behind those things from which he turned away, and he runs back upon those sins which he left. And of those hearing these things, whether catechumens who left the gentile life or faithful already advanced in stretching forward to the things ahead, if the life has become wretched, they say nothing other than: 'We will go behind our turnings-away, and each will do the pleasing things of his evil heart.' For there is an evil heart and there is a good heart. Therefore let no one go 'behind his turnings-away' nor do 'the pleasing things of his evil heart.'

'Therefore,' toward those answering these things, 'says the Lord: Ask now among the nations: Who has heard such fearful things which virgin Israel has done exceedingly?' If the church from the nations asks among the nations, it will be said: Hear what fearful things virgin Israel has done. For let us compare the life of those who sinned with the life of those who turned and believed, and we will know that those did fearful things, killing 'the Lord of glory,' but these turned to him who was killed and died by those for the sins of the world.
translator_notes: ἀποστροφαί: turnings-away (from evil)—walking behind them is relapse.

title: Three springs: rock, Lebanon, Spirit
english: 'Will breasts fail from a rock, or snow from Lebanon? Or will water carried violently by wind turn aside? For my people forgot me; they burned incense in vain…' Here he has spoken differences of waters: first 'Will breasts fail from a rock?'; second 'or snow from Lebanon?'; third 'Will water carried violently by wind turn aside?' These three kinds of waters are the springs which the soul of the righteous, made like the deer, longs for: 'In the manner the deer longs for the springs of the waters, so my soul longs toward you, O God.'

Who has become a deer hostile to the race of serpents? Who so thirsted for God as to say: 'My soul thirsted toward the living God'? Who so thirsted for the breasts of the rock? 'And the rock was Christ.' Who so thirsted for Holy Spirit? If we do not thirst for the three springs, we will not find even one. Jews seemed to thirst for one spring, of God; but since they did not thirst for the Christ and the Holy Spirit, they do not drink even from God. Those from the heresies seemed to thirst for Christ Jesus; but since they did not thirst for the Father, God of law and prophets, they drink neither from Jesus Christ. And those who keep one God but despise the prophecies did not thirst for the Holy Spirit in the prophets; therefore they drink neither from the paternal spring nor from the one who cried in the temple: 'If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.'

Therefore breasts from a rock do not fail. But those abandoned a spring of living water; a spring did not abandon them. God distances himself from no one, but those distancing themselves from him will perish; God rather draws near and meets the one coming toward him. When the son who ate up the substance returned, the father met him. 'I am a God who draws near, and not a God from far off, says the Lord.' Therefore 'breasts from a rock will not fail'—the waters of Jesus—'or snow from Lebanon'—the paternal waters. And there is snow coming down from Lebanon, in the manner of the water of the Holy Spirit: 'Will water carried violently by wind turn aside?' It does not turn aside; but each of us when sinning himself becomes a fugitive from drinking from the Holy Spirit.

title: Incense in vain; do not appear empty
english: 'For my people forgot me; they burned incense in vain.' Everyone who sins has forgotten God, but the righteous says: 'All these things came upon us, and we did not forget you.' And what is 'they burned incense in vain' must be understood. If we take up again the one hundred fortieth Psalm—'Let my prayer become as incense before you'—we will understand. Prayer compounded of a fine heart, when our heart is not thickened, being sent up becomes as incense before God.

If then the prayer of the righteous is incense before God, the prayer of the unjust is incense indeed, but such that it could be said: 'they burned incense in vain'—as about Judas: 'Let his prayer become unto sin.' That one according to praying burned incense in vain. And who burns incense in vain—understand still more thus. 'Three times of the year every male of yours will be seen before the Lord your God,' to which is immediately added: 'You will not be seen before me empty.' Therefore of those coming to be seen, one must not appear empty before the Lord.
translator_notes: Greek witness for end of §18.10 is lacunose in the locked crib; Pass B stops with the intact sense.

title: Ask Jesus to open the reading
english: That mind of Scripture becomes present to the eye that has room for the clear sense of the holy writings. I have said this first to wake myself and you who hear, that we may pay attention to the reading and ask Jesus to come, show himself to us, and teach us what is written in this place.
translator_notes: Opening of Homily 19 is lacunose in the locked Greek; Pass B follows the surviving sense.

title: Pashhur strikes Jeremiah and is named Migrant
english: Jeremiah prophesied, and Pashhur son of Immer the priest heard the words of the prophecy. And though, as is likely upon the bare sequence of the prophecy, many had heard Jeremiah, it is not quickly written that another heard except Pashhur. And Scripture cared to say also whose son he was—that of Immer—and that he was called a priest, and what rank he had among the people—that he had been appointed leading the house of the Lord at the time Jeremiah was prophesying these words.

And it is written that hearing the words of this prophecy Pashhur struck Jeremiah, and was not content with having struck him, but also threw him into a certain fall-pit. Scripture cared to say also where this fall-pit was—in the gate of Benjamin—and that the fall-pit was in a place where there was an upper room, and an upper room of no other than the house of the Lord. These things the Holy Spirit wrote as having come to be upon the prophecy to Jeremiah, and as having come from Pashhur.

Then it says: on the next day Pashhur led Jeremiah out of the fall-pit. And led out, Jeremiah said to Pashhur that the Lord did not call you this name Pashhur; another name has been set for you—as for Jacob, Israel; as for Abram, Abraham; as for Sarai, Sarah—so he has set for you the name Migrant. And for this reason he called you Migrant, because the Lord says: Behold, I give you into migration with all—with whom? Not with your wife and your sons and your daughters, but with your friends. And when you are given into migration, your friends will fall by a sword. Then, as there is a difference for those falling by a sword if they fall by a sword of enemies or by a sword of others, he says that the friends of the one who threw Jeremiah into the fall-pit will fall into a sword of their enemies. And your eyes, he says, will see these things prophesied. But you and all Judah I will give into the hands of the king of Babylon, after your friends suffer these things, and they will migrate them into Babylon and will cut them down; for the king of Judah and those from Judah they will cut down with a sword, and no longer is 'of their enemies' added, as upon the former who were said to be friends of Pashhur. Then he says: and I will give all the strength of this city and all the treasures of the king of Judah and all the labors of this city into the hands of their enemies.
translator_notes: Μέτοικος / Pashhur renamed Migrant (Jer 20:3).

title: Striking the prophet; Christ still gives his back
english: The enchanters of the Egyptians also had rods that wanted to refute the rods of Moses and Aaron as not being from God. But the rods from God overturn those of the sophists and enchanters; 'Aaron’s swallowed them'—for it alone was enough for this even without Moses’ rod. So then Pashhur 'struck Jeremiah the prophet,' and with character: 'and he struck Jeremiah the prophet.' 'The prophet' is also added. Here then the one who struck struck Jeremiah the prophet.

And it is written in Acts that someone struck Paul, ordered by Ananias the high priest. Therefore Paul said: 'God is about to strike you, whitewashed wall.' And until now Ebionites, ordered by an unlawful high-priestly word, strike the apostle of Jesus Christ with blasphemous words. And Paul says toward such a high-priestly word: 'God is about to strike you.' And such a high priest is handsome on the surface and a whitewashed wall.

Christ says: 'I have given my back to scourges, and my cheeks to blows, and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spit.' The simple know these things only of that time when Pilate scourged him, when Jews planned against him. But I see Jesus daily 'giving his back to scourges.' Go into the synagogues of the Jews and see Jesus scourged by them with the tongue of blasphemy. See those gathered from the nations planning against Christians, how they take Jesus, and there too he 'gives his own back to scourges.' Consider the Word of God being insulted, spoken ill of, hated by the unbelievers. See that 'he gave his cheeks to blows,' and having taught that if someone strikes you on the cheek turn also the other, he himself does it. So many strike and scourge him, and he is silent and does not speak. For it is written that he does not speak when being scourged. And 'until now Jesus has not turned his face away from the shame of spit.'

title: The upper room and the fall-pit
english: It followed upon the prophet having been struck to narrate those struck—for example the apostle and if anyone else has been struck—and to set beside them also the things about Jesus himself. So 'Pashhur struck Jeremiah the prophet and threw him into the fall-pit which was in the Benjamin gate of the upper room.' The fall-pit of Benjamin was of the upper room. Benjamin’s allotment is Jerusalem, in which is the temple of God, as the one able to hear the divine readings will find from the allotment written in Joshua. Since then the temple was in Benjamin’s allotment, which is interpreted Son of the right hand (for there is nothing leftward about the temple of God), for this reason this one throws 'into the fall-pit which was in the Benjamin gate of the upper room of the Lord’s house.' While there is an 'upper room in the Lord’s house' he 'threw' the prophet 'into the fall-pit.'

And we beg that taking Jeremiah now we may bring him up into the upper room 'in the Lord’s house.' And I will show from Scripture that the upper room is the high and lifted mind, when it bears witness to the holy ones that they received the prophets into upper rooms. In the third of Kingdoms a widow receiving Elijah the prophet in Zarephath of Sidon lodged the prophet 'into her upper room.' And in the fourth the one receiving Elisha prepared a house for him into the upper room. But sinful Ahaziah fell from the upper room. And Jesus also commands you not to come down from the housetop. For he says: when these and these things happen, 'then let the one on the housetop not come down to take the things from his house.' The one fleeing in persecutions is not told not to go up onto a housetop, but from the housetop 'not to come down to take the things from his house.'

It is good then to be in upper rooms, good to be on housetops and somehow to be above. And the wonderful apostles also, as is written of them in Acts, when being together they were free for prayers and the word of God, were in an upper room. And since they were in an upper room, they were not below. For this reason 'tongues as of fire distributed appeared to them.' But Peter also, when he was sending up the prayer to God, 'went up onto the housetop'; and if he had not gone up onto the housetop, he would not have seen 'a vessel as a sheet coming down from heaven, let down by four corners from heaven.' And Tabitha also who did the alms...
translator_notes: Section ends mid-example in locked crib; sense kept within Pass A.

title: Tomorrow he is led out; friends fall by the sword
english: 'And it came to be on the next day, and Pashhur led Jeremiah out of the fall-pit.' O Lord Jesus, come again; make these things clear also to me and to those who have come upon the spiritual food. How on 'the next day' does he himself lead 'Jeremiah out of the fall-pit'? For as long as today’s day stands—and today is this whole age—the sinner throws the prophet down into the fall-pit; but if the present day ceases and tomorrow comes, then having repented he leads him out from the fall-pit.

Then Jeremiah says to him what Pashhur will suffer. What does he say to him? 'Not Pashhur did he call your name, but Migrant. For thus says the Lord.' This Pashhur is about to be migrated according to the worth of the sins into Babylon—not alone, but also with his friends. For he is handed over to Nebuchadnezzar and goes away into Confusion and is punished for his sins, since 'he threw the prophet into the fall-pit.' Who then are the friends of Pashhur, the namesake of Blackness of mouth? All who have received his words, who have been blackened together with his blackened mouth, who have received doctrines of blackness. 'And they will fall by a sword of their enemies.' Those appointed over punishments—these are the ones who have the swords and make them fall; concerning whom the word prophesies and says: 'And your eyes will see.' These prophesied things, he says, 'your eyes will see.'

'And you and all Judah I will give into the hands of the king of Babylon.' Whoever of Judah is caught so sinful as to be worthy of the king of Babylon, of Confusion, will be handed over to him. And the king of Babylon receives those who sin. And the king of Babylon according to the history is Nebuchadnezzar, but according to the ascent is the evil one. And to this one the sinner is handed over, since he is both enemy and avenger. And that the sinner is handed over to him, let Paul teach you, where on the one hand he says about Hymenaeus and Alexander: 'whom I handed over to Satan,' and about the one who has fornicated: 'when you are gathered and my spirit with the power of the Lord Jesus, I have judged to hand over such a one to Satan for destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved.'
translator_notes: Pashhur etymology: blackness of mouth (μέλαν στόμα).
Babylon = Confusion on the ascent.

title: You deceived me, Lord—and the fire in the bones
english: And indeed the one section has been completed, and already let us begin also the second; for it has matters straightway from the first reading that are not ordinary. And attending to the wording again we will ask Jesus to come, and we will beg him to come more manifestly and more brightly, that coming he may teach all of us whether the prophet spoke truly—as it befits one to think about a prophet—in what follows, or lying, which it is not lawful to say about a holy prophet.

And he says toward God: 'You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived; you prevailed and were strong; I became a laugh; all the day I continued being sneered at… for the word of the Lord became a reproach to me and a jeer all day. And I said: I will by no means name the name of the Lord, and I will by no means speak still upon his name. And it became in my heart as a fire burning, burning in my bones, and I am exhausted from every side and cannot bear it, because I heard the blame of many gathered around,' saying: 'Conspire, and let us conspire against him…' But while those say these things the prophet says: 'And the Lord is with me as a strong fighter; therefore they pursued and could not understand; they were greatly ashamed…' This is the second section of the reading.

How then does the prophet say: 'You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived'? Does God deceive? How I will manage the word, I am at a loss. Ceasing from being deceived the prophet says: 'You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived,' as of an elementary schooling and introduction having come to be for him in a deception, and he being unable to be schooled and introduced into piety unless first he is deceived, that later he may come to perceive the deception. And it is enough only to say a useful example for what lies before us. We speak to children leading the children, and we do not speak as to perfect ones, but as to children needing education we speak to them, and we deceive the children, frightening them, that the lack of education among children may cease.
